Rating: A Beautiful Mind - ***/****
Decent movie, fine acting, some clever stuff... but just, frankly a bit bland. This coming from an econ major who hears about Nash this and Nash that in class...

I don't know... I have yet to see a "biopic" attempting to cover a broad swath of someone's life that I really truly liked (true-story movies that cover smaller periods of time fare better in my mind). Oh well.

[size=3]Ron Howard's Oscar-winning tearjerker is about a schizophrenic man, John Nash, who had a brilliant career in mathematics while overcoming his own inner demons. The movie is reveling in its own good intentions...it's a typical Oscar-grubber, and the Academy fell for it. Certainly, the film is marginally entertaining, and it does feature a stellar supporting performance from Jennifer Connelly as Nash's wife. But Russell Crowe, an actor I frequently have admired, is far too dependent on mannerisms and tics to convey his torment. And Howard's limited imagination simply can not convey the sheer horror of schizophrenia. Howard's version of mental confusion is three convenient characters who pop up from time to time, each clearly representing a facet of Nash's psyche. Although I am not an expert on schizophrenia by any means, I doubt that it manifests itself in such simple ways. The film's failure to grasp the mental illness that is its subject would be forgiveable if it at least had originality or wit...but [i]A Beautiful Mind [/i]is content to stay within the confines of a classic Hollywood melodrama. It does not even trust its audience enough to explain the mathematical theories that led to Nash winning the Nobel Prize. Naturally, we would not need a detailed explanation, but something more than just a few statements like "You've changed the face of modern economics." The one thing that [i]A Beautiful Mind [/i]succeeds at is presenting the point-of-view of a person who watches a loved one descend into mental illness. But as an evocation of that illness, and a biography of John Nash, the film fails. Howard has become a true Hollywood poster-child, much more so than Steven Spielberg. While Spielberg continues to experiment, Howard is content to stay within formulas. [i]A Beautiful Mind [/i]was a winning formula for Howard with audiences and critics, but I remain unconvinced.[/size]

[b][font=Verdana][size=2]A BEAUTIFUL MIND (2001)

[/b][u]THE GOOD:[/u]

--Akiva Goldsmanperhaps the biggest surprise of this entire film experience. "A Beautiful Mind", a brilliantly written film comes from the same person who wrote one of 1998's worst movies, "The Avengers". His improvement with screenplay writing is astounding. I hope Goldsman continues to deliver such good films like this one.

--The story of a man haunted by delusions coming from his own mind is compelling and kept me glued to the screen.

--The brilliant performances in this film must be mentioned. Russell's Crowe and Jennifer Connelly vividly bring to life John and Alicia, both delivering powerhouse performances. Their chemistry is incredible. Ed Harris is very effective on a number of different levels as Parcher, Christopher Plummer is extremely accurate and believable as Dr Rosen and Paul Bettany brings charm and zest to the role of Charles Herman.

--The twist that takes place in the middle of the film caught me completely off guard. I was definitely surprised and definitely didn't see it coming. Looking back on the film after knowing what happens is very interesting, there are subtle hints at the twist that is coming (loved the girl running through the birds - how on Earth did they do that?).

--James Horner's score for this film can be described in no other way than completely and utterly beautiful. I also loved the song "All Love Can Be", performed by Charlotte Church.

--The makeup is very good, it was very accurate and I loved seeing the several techniques they used to make Russell and Jennifer older. It didn't even look like the actors at the end of the movie - now that's great makeup.

--The love story is really what "A Beautiful Mind" is all about and it delivers on this front in an incredible fashion. This will remembered over time as one of the best and most effective 'love conquers all' films. 

[u]THE BAD:[/u]

--Though still good, I found the film's first 30-35 minutes less engaging and slightly lagging.

--I know for a fact that John Forbes Nash was not as innocent as he appears in this film, and I for one would've liked to have seen some of the dark side of the man of which I hear so frequently about in reviews.

--It bothered me that they put so much effort in making Crowe look a lot older, but Josh Lucas' Martin didn't look too different when Crowe had aged a good 25-30 years.

[u]RATING:[/u]

9/10 - A very, very high 9/10. "A Beautiful Mind" was a brilliant showcase of love conquers all, one of 2001's best movies.

 I cant believe this film was nominated for Best Picture. The thing is such a walking cliche. no seriously I cant think of an original moment in the entire film. Yeah I know the story is one told a thousand times, so I wasnt expecting ground breaking originality , but still every single movement struck me as a cliche. I found the film very predictable, like Road to Perdition predictable, like I was saying dialog before the characters were. the final scene played out, down to the dialog, precisely how I thought it was going to happen. there was no surprise or life to anything. To me this destroyed all the drama in it, all emotion, and all deeper meaning. At risk at sounding callous, I was bored more than I was moved; In the Bedroom almost put me in the bedroom. the direction and dialog were just relentlessly mediocre and frankly overly unmistakable in its meaning and direction that it leaked from my brain with in hours of seeing the film. with that being said, all the actors bring a lot to the table and make the film almost compelling.
  
  A Beautiful Mind
  
 I dont know what is up with Crowe being in undeserving Best Picture winners but A Beautiful Mind was barely good. There are moments in the film that contain such on the nose dialog that is broader line appalling. (like wise moments of directorial unsubtly) For example, the conversation between the doctor and Alicia, or the bedroom talk between Nash and his wife. Opies direction was safe, unassuming and relentlessly pedestrian. In fact my biggest problem with A Beautiful Mind comes from how conventional it is. to quote Desson Thornson, [its] one of those formulaically rendered Important Subject Movies. I hate the score. really, I cant think of a more obtuse, obvious, grating and manipulative score at the moment. (through I am writing this at 5 oclock in the morning, and I havent slept in awhile.) now, I really think Crowe did a great job in this film, and I wish he won over Washington. Likewise, Connelly was great (through to say she did better than Maggie Smith is criminal). Nash, or at least the movie version of him, is a great, and tragic character, and he makes the film worth-while. I also enjoy how the film put the viewer in Nashs shoes by the twist.
  
  Moulin Rouge!
  
 good lord, how divided I am on this film. the first time I saw it I watched about ten minutes, turned it off and went what the hell was that? (Im being literal). the second time I tried watching it I got about 15 minutes in, turned off and said what the hell was that? well, I tried again, and on the proverbial third time I made it all the way through, and said Im not sure if I like that or not. well, I have since then seen it many times and I have change that, if I may quote the Duke, to generally, I like. the thing is I both adore, and loathe, the style of the film. it is a such a cerebration of life, love and music that the thing has so much heart that [i]loving[/i] the film is very easy. but then again the film is such an shameless exercise in style, spectacle and shallowness that [i]hating [/i]it is very easy as well. (for the record I have the save dilemma with Kill Bill, abate to a lesser degree, because I find Bill less spectacle and deeper through I hate using that word in relation to both. also, MR! doesn't seem aware that it is all style, where as KB uses self-awareness of it being all style as style) my main problem with the film is it needs to calm down. for example if the editing was every .5 second instead of every .25 second (hyperbole, I know) the thing would seem less like a ADHD kid that forgot to take his medicine. if I may quote Alex for a moment, Baz Luhrmann must vomit rainbows. while I dont agree to the extent of this which Alex takes it too, I think the meaning behind it is true. somewhere, some how Lurhmann should have made the screen only 99.5% full(again hyperbole but still). ok, with that out of the way, I really, really, really, like the humor in this film. every joke clicks with me, and that is one of the reasons I generally...like it. I LOVE Kidman in this, and I would be more than ok with her winning instead of Ms. Berry. the rest of the cast does stellar as well. the songs, and dances, work for me, but I wish some of them where more show tune-like than pop. about half of me wants to give this film a 10, about an 1/8 of me a 0, and the rest a 7. so Im giving it an 8. (Im sure that doesnt work at mathematically.)
  
  Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring
  
 ok, I could talk about the impressive production values of the film, the lush camera work, the impressive costumes and art direction, the great special effects or the number things that were invented for it. or maybe I could mention a screenplay that does the impossible, or how Jackson draws the viewer in with seductive power. but really, now that is so commonly thought it would kinda redundant. the reason why I dont think FOTR deserved the Oscar is, of all the trilogy, FOTR is the one that could have been tightened up the most (not that I want to do so), and the least important to the entire trilogy. FOTR is an extended introduction. while it is a great introduction, it is still just an introduction. Im glad the Oscar saved it for the real meat of the trilogy 
  
  Gosford Park
  
 there are so many reasons why I love this film that I could literally talk about it forever, so Ill try to keep this relatively short. First, Gosford Park draws the viewer in with seductive power; by the time I got to the first drawing room scene I was so wrapped up in the characters lives that I really do have a hard time understanding why someone finds the movie boring. part of this is how Altman infuses such authentic energy into the film that it doesnt feel like a film Second, the acting is nothing short breathtaking. I have never seen a film where every actor on the screen set it on fire and that is precisely what the ensemble does here. Maggie Smith should have won the Oscar for Lady Trentham, and more of the cast should have garnered recognition. Third, Altman, aided by Fellows screenplay, tells each plot, subplot and story with such grace, economy and simple elegance that it paints a 360 degree picture of class, and it relation to social behavior that brilliant is the only word that is fit to describe it. the way it handles exposition alone is amazing as there is not one pure sentence of exposition, every line turns a scene. every action taken by a character relates to class in someway. Forth, the film can be viewed from a number of angles and be at least satisfactory. one can look at it as a murder mystery, and while it isnt the hardest to guess the ending, nor the most complex ever written it still works decently enough to be entertaining. you can view it as a comedy of manners (or satire), and the film works beautifully. there are moments of such bite that it hurts. for example, why does one have to do these things? or the classic piece of music over the picnic. you can view it as a drama about the effects of rigidly defined class structures. the moment between Mrs. Croft and Mrs. Wilson is one of the most moving scenes I have seen in an ensemble film, and when Jennings looked himself in the mirror I cried. I have never done that before with any film. you could view the film as dramedy and come up with a social commentary. Finally, you can simple view it as Altman showing off, after all who else tells stories that have 30 main characters?
  
  or you can, like me, view it as all of the above.
  
 there are two other features I wish to discuss. first is the general wit in the dialog. I dont know who said this but I remember hearing years ago, only the English can make an insult sound like a compliment without trying and the dialog proves it. I cant name the number of times a person insults another using kind words, the two clear examples are it must be so disappointing when something just flops like that? and well, thats marvelous. apart from this Fellows dialog is extremely quotable, funny, and period sounding without sounding forced. I call that wit. second, Gosford Park is a film filled with irony, and frankly I wish more films used this device. while the thing is a relentless attack on using class as a rigid definition, and attacks those who do so, the film feels sorry for them; while it paints Trentham negatively, you sense a sadness for what she should be. to point out just one moment of sublime irony is enough I think so; during the murder scene, Ivor asks Mabel to sit with him while he plays a song. this simple act is the turning point in her arch, from here out she is no longer pushed around by her husband. the only reason this happens, the only reason why it is as meaningful, is because Ivor is a celebrity; in other words, class, or social standing, was a big positive. This act occurs in a scene in which Trentham is bossing people around, thanks to her standing, William is being murdered, thanks to his social standing, the upstairs people are generally disinterested in great music because it is beneath them. (it even goes further by having all the downstairs people interested in the music, forming the subtext of them looking to the future while upstairs are stuck in the past) in other words, class, or social standing is a huge negative. that I call sublime irony.

Russell Crowe is an amazing actor with an uncanny ability to get inside a character's skin. It's obvious there is no thought involved when he's working -- he simply steps inside the character, sees through his eyes, feels what he feels, and thus breathes life into him. He also has a unique talent for playing tragic figures, revealing a deep sadness beneath layers of frustration and masculine self-consciousness. His characters are so empathetic that the experience transcends the natural detachment between audience and fictional storyline... you feel connected to his characters as to a real person, with the same intimacy and immediacy you'd feel for friends or family. When I watched A Beautiful Mind, I felt so much heartbreak and empathy, I wanted to step into the movie and rescue him. Watching The Insider last night, I felt the same protective urge, as I found myself thinking, "If anything bad happens to him, I'm going to be upset. They just better not mess with him." It's ridiculous and irrational, but that's the power of Crowe's acting; he bypasses your head and goes straight for your heart. I suspect this is why so many women find him irresistible, even though he's a drunken, belligerent, misogynistic slob.

Crowe is the lifeblood of this movie; without him it would be in danger of becoming an intellectual exercise. With him it's a fairly astonishing dramatic piece, with a full complement of excellent acting, storytelling, cinematography, etc. Al Pacino takes on an atypically soft and sophisticated persona, and, more typically, he plays the heck out of the role. His presence is a perfect counterpoint to Crowe's; the friendship between their characters holds the movie together, and keeps it grounded through what might otherwise be a gratuitous philosophical dialogue. Anyone who thinks this movie is purely political misses the point. Yes, it paints an ugly picture of corporate corruption. But a larger theme overarches the politics; an elegant, powerful story about honor and responsibility, about making hard choices, about the consequences of lying and the consequences of telling the truth. In the end, the movie's somewhat awkward intellectualism gives way to a simple, touching portrait of a basic human conflict... the longing to devote our life's work to something meaningful, the deep need to immerse ourselves in the love of our families, and the hard fact that these two drives sometimes pull us painfully in opposite directions.

A Beautiful Mind manages to twist enough pathos out of John Nash's incredible life story to redeem an at-times goofy portrayal of schizophrenia. Russell Crowe tackles the role with characteristic fervor, playing the Nobel prize-winning mathematician from his days at Princeton, where he developed a groundbreaking economic theory, to his meteoric rise to the cover of Forbes magazine and an MIT professorship, and on through to his eventual dismissal due to schizophrenic delusions. Of course, it is the delusions that fascinate director Ron Howard and, predictably, go astray. Nash's other world, populated as it is by a maniacal Department of Defense agent (Ed Harris), an imagined college roommate who seems straight out of Dead Poets Society, and an orphaned girl, is so fluid and scriptlike as to make the viewer wonder if schizophrenia is really as slick as depicted.

[size=2]Continuing with my look back at past Best Picture Winners are two more recent Oscar winners. 

The Academy Award Winner for Best Picture for 2001 went to [b]A Beautiful Mind[/b]. The other nominees for Best Picture included [i]Gosford Park[/i], [i]In the Bedroom[/i], [i]Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring[/i], and [i]Moulin Rouge[/i]. Other notable films include [i]Training Day,[/i] [i]Mulholland Dr.,[/i] [i]Memento[/i], [i]Monster's Ball[/i], [i]Iris[/i], [i]Shrek[/i], [i]Ghost World[/i], [i]The Royal Tenenbaums[/i], [i]Amelie[/i], and [i]Bridget Jones Diary[/i].

 

Directed by Ron Howard, [b]A Beautiful Mind[/b] is the story of John Nash, a brilliant [/size][font=Times New Roman][size=3]mathematician [/size][/font][size=2]and professor who also suffers from schizophrenia. Russell Crowe plays Nash, who we first see as a gruff, awkward and anti-social college student. He writes mathematical formulas on his dorm room window, doesn't fit in with the guys, and has no clue on who to approach women. Ron Howard (in a twist for him) doesn't immediatly reveal his mental illness, although it's not difficult for the viewer to realize there is something more going on with the unlikable, asocial Nash. A few years later, when Nash is well-known for his theories, he is recruited by CIA agent Parcher (Ed Harris) to help solve Soviet military codes. It doesn't take Einstein for the viewer to figure outt what's happening by now. Along the way Nash meets a beautiful student named Alicia (Jennifer Connelly) who soon becomes his wife. Soon afterwards Alicia realizes there is something more to Nash's bizarre behavior, and John winds up in a mental hospital. When he comes home he continues to act in a bizarre fashion. This film was a huge disappointment for me on so many levels. Ron Howard is one of Hollywood's most conventional directors. John Nash was anything but conventional. Directed by Rob Marshall, [b]Chicago [/b]is the screen adaption of the popular Broadway musical. Set in the 1920's, Roxie Hart (Renee Zellweger) is a young woman unhappily married to Amos (John C. Reilly) who desires to be a vaudeville star. Roxie idolizes Velma Kelly (Catherine Zeta-Jones) and is having an affair with a man named Fred Casley (Dominic West) that promises to make her as big a star as Velma. When he gets violent, Roxie shoots him. Initially Amos agrees to take the fall until he finds out Roxie was having an affair. Once in prison, Roxie is surprised to find that Velma is also there. Both hook up with superstar lawyer Billy Flynn (Richard Gere) who has never lost a case. Flynn's strategy is to create a media circus behind each case, garnering public support for his defendants. At the same time Roxie and Velma compete for Flynn's attention, and most importantly the limelight in this media circus.

Simply said, [b]Chicago[/b] is a delight. Where most musicals fail to transfer successfully to the big screen, [i]Chicago [/i]strikes a perfect balance with a compelling enough story for the big screen and well placed and performed musical numbers. Catherine Zeta-Jones looks like she belongs on the stage, she's a great dancer and has a wonderful voice. Renee Zellweger is alternately sweet and sassy, always a delight watch. Richard Gere, Queen Latifah and John C. Reilly are also very good. Never a dull moment in this quickly paced film. Although I loved [i]The Pianist[/i], I have no complaints with this Best Picture Winner. [i]

It is a hard impulse to deny, as both geniuses and the insane are defined primarily in how they differ from "ordinary" people. Both are somehow removed from the everyday in extraordinary/terrible ways, so the urge to see them as two sides of the same coin is difficult to stifle completely. It lurks constantly in the background of our thoughts on the truly exceptional, and it pops up repeatedly in popular depictions of the troubled lives of the imminent. Ron Howard's A Beautiful Mind, which tells the story of Nobel Prize-winning mathematical genius and paranoid schizophrenic John Forbes Nash, Jr., constantly plays with this line, but the film succeeds largely because it avoids conflating Forbes' brilliance and his mental illness, instead focusing on how the latter was an encumbrance on the former. It has been suggested, quite rightly, that the same unique mental predisposition that allowed Forbes to imagine the solution to complex mathematical quandaries in ways no other human being had been able to do also contributed to his sinking into paranoid hysteria and delusions. Yet, to say that they are one in the same, or to try to romanticize the schizophrenia as somehow being an enabling factor for his imminence, is a discredit to Forbes and a risky delusion in itself. Nash first gained a name for himself at Princeton in the late 1940s, where he wrote a master's thesis that essentially revised 150 years of economic theory and eventually became the bedrock for future works in disciplines as disparate as gaming theory and physics. A Beautiful Mind begins here, with Russell Crowe playing Forbes as many have described him: arrogant, aloof, socially inept, and always in search of the true original idea. Disdainful of classroom learning, Nash was an individual in every sense of the word, a misanthrope who was fully aware of the fact that others didn't like him very much. Crowe plays up Nash's uncharismatic tendencies in a way that assures us that Nash is not to be sentimentalized, but not to the point that he becomes unbearable. The screenplay by Akiva Goldsman, based on the critically lauded biography by Sylvia Nasar, is clever in how it deals with the onset of Nash's schizophrenia, and those who are familiar with Nash's life story will immediately recognize the primary mechanism by which it works. Those who don't know Nash's life will likely enjoy the film the most, as it is designed to put you in his shoes and see his life from his point of view. In some instances, this involves rather laborious special effects that are designed to visualize his thought processes, whether that be matching the patterns of light created by sunlight refracting through the cut-glass surface of a tumbler to the design on a bad tie, or recognizing hidden codes in newspaper articles. Sometimes this works (as when Nash looks at a wall of numbers and discerns the repeating pattern), sometimes it is just silly (as in the scene where he describes the mathematically rationalized process by which three men can score with three women at a bar). Like Nasar's biography, A Beautiful Mind is structured in three acts: genius, madness, and awakening. Nash's early days at Princeton produced his greatest works, and by the time he was in his early 20s, he had a coveted position at MIT. There, he meets a beautiful graduate student named Alicia (Jennifer Connelly), who somehow understands his eccentric, isolated ways of life and falls in love with and marries him. Then, Nash becomes involved in code-breaking for the government under the auspices of a shadowy CIA operative named William Parcher (Ed Harris), which leads him into a world of increasing fear and paranoia, to the point that he can no longer discern what is real and what is not. It is at this point that his schizophrenia reveals itself in its full-blown state, and much of what Nash thought was real turns out to be the production of his own mind. The film is at its most compelling when Nash is battling hardest against the forces within himself. There is a deep-seated irony that this isolated man finds his greatest rival inside his own mind, the very place that spawned his mathematical brilliance - it is the great tragedy that the rational and the irrational emerged from the same place, thus making the latter so much more believable for him. Again, the danger here is in seeing them as one and the same, but A Beautiful Mind constantly avoids this pitfall by placing them against each other, showing how the intellectual production of Nash the genius could only continue once he willed himself to control the impulses of Nash the schizophrenic. As Nash is constantly haunted by his delusions, the film never pretends (as some will accuse it of doing) of painting Nash as a miracle case who, by dent of the love of Alicia and others, "overcomes" his mental illness. It is true that, starting in the early 1990s, Nash's schizophrenia did go into remission, a rare occurrence for a mental illness that is generally degenerative in nature. The film uses this miracle of sorts in an expected feel-good kind of way, but by this point it has earned the right to do so. A Beautiful Mind is conventional (and NOT the best film of 2001, at all) in its narrative arc of transcending great obstacles, but Crowe's carefully nuanced portrayal of Nash, Connelly's fully transformation into her own as an actor and Howard's avoidance of cheap sentimentalism balances any overly audience-arousing histrionics the film throws our way toward the end, most notably when Nash is awarded the Nobel prize for mathematics in 1994. Depicting mental states is a difficult thing to do in film, particularly in popular films, and if A Beautiful Mind simplifies Nash's condition, it is in the pursuit of the genuine cinematic, something for which it cannot be blamed. If you want to know the in-depth details of Nash's life and his bout with schizophrenia, read Nasar's excellent book. If you want an engaging, rousing, well-made film about a brilliant man whose life was almost completely devastated by mental illness, see A Beautiful Mind.

I don't like Russell Crowe.  I never really have.  I certainly don't think he needs two assistants in this movie (and a trainer, apparently) while Jennifer Connelly, who is arguably both more talented and better looking, has none.  I'd rather like to clonk him on the head with his [i]Gladiator[/i] Oscar before reassigning it to Tom Hanks for [i]Cast Away[/i], which was a better and more demanding performance.

I also don't know much about John Nash, the real John Nash.  His is, for a start, not a field in which I'm particularly gifted.  I'm sure I heard his name before this movie came out--I do try to keep myself posted on who wins Nobel prizes--I'm equally certain that I didn't retain the information.

I can, however, identify with the fictional John Nash presented to us in the person of an actor I don't like.

No, I'm not schizophrenic, thank gods.  My symptoms support a very different diagnosis indeed.  I have never had hallucinations.  I am not (usually) a danger to myself or others.  

But everyone who's both creative and mentally ill knows the fear shown us by this movie.  [i]What if the meds take away my gift?  What if I get better, but I'm no good?[/i]  We live in fear of this.  All of my past roommates may be real (I have either pictures or video of the lot of 'em, and where I don't, I have people who've met 'em), but I can burst into tears while playing computer solitaire.  I can get so angry at people without inside voices that I nearly kill them.  And if the meds work, if the meds make me stable, what if I can't write anymore?

You have to understand that I don't do a heck of a lot of writing now.  These reviews are pretty much it.  I have a diary, but I don't even write much in that.  But I'm good, and I've always been good, and what if the meds work and I'm not?  Would it be better to live with the anger and the tears and the rest of the whirl and maybe, just maybe, be great?

There are a lot of flaws to [i]A Beautiful Mind[/i], apparently the more so if you really do know about the life of the real John Nash.  (I understand the math's right, at least.)  I happen to know that they left a lot of things out.  They always do; you can't not.  But oh, they got the fear right.

However, you feel sympathatic when you see that the drugs to subdue his illness has an affect on his intelligence and he is faced between his intelligence and his family. Anyone who has been close to the frailties of the human mind will appreciate how respectfully and honestly this film approaches the subject. Howard is able to portray all the complex reactions to mental illness while maintaining the humanity and dignity of the patient. Superbly directed, wonderfully acted by Russell Crowe and cast, film succeeds on every level.

I knew nothing about John Nash before seeing this, so Goldsman's story and Howard's direction did keep surprising me. With Ed Harris and Jennifer Connelly having starring roles I was afraid for a moment it might be like Pollock, but it is not a fair comparison. It is a little misleading that Harris is given top billing because as an agent from a shadowy CIA-type organization he really does not have very much screen time. Connelly shines much brighter in the role of Alicia, Nash's eventual wife. Paul Bettany is wonderful as Nash's college roommate. Lucas, Goldberg, Rapp and Gray-Stanford are some of his classmates and eventual co-workers. They all turn in great supporting performances. There are several attention grabbing shots and effects too. Russell Crowe subtly ages as we observe most of Nash's adult life. I was caught up in his life story as things seem to be going well. It did take some time to adjust when I began to realize the effect the schizophrenia had on the way Nash saw his world, and therefore the way Howard leads us, the audience, to see his life. The movie has moments of humor, tension and romance. It is good to see a person get the support and help they need to overcome mental illness.

A Beautiful Mind is literally a mind-blowing affair that will compel every one of us to explore feverishly the human mind in all its potential for success and failure, happiness and misery, hope and reality. Russell Crowe is phenomenal in portraying Nash's obsession, genius, and physical destruction amidst mental construction while Jennifer Connelly is absolutely captivating with her charming screen presence and powerful performance. Ed Harris plays his character well in achieving that cold and heartless persona that will yield at nothing in establishing his purpose in life. A Beautiful Mind is thrilling not only in the action-packed-Sylvester Stalone action sequences but also in the quieter and more sensitive examination of the logical and realistic self against the illogical ego, the rationality of mathematics versus the irrationality of love, and the harmony of the mind, body, and soul. A highly recommended movie that is engaging, stirring, and extremely rich.

The movie didn't really dwell on the cause of his madness. The documentary film however said it began when he was trying to solve an unsolvable or improbably solvable problem known by mathmeticians.... kind of a rubic cube thing that challenges the most gifted people.

SEE the PBS version, a far better film and more accurate too here:

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b5Y74lKhPlA


[img]https://encrypted-tbn2.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcT8sQi7-cB3Qu9Gd71g0sl3N-9cdF7CZ_5-Isgm7W8zrEriXqP_[/img]
 
He was interested in game theory, which the chess board like thing they play games with ( pebbles, white and black), provided basis for his new thinking about strategy.
 
Cryptography, solving all those numbers on the wall at the Pentagon, and reading newspapers for them for clues.... all of that could have been in his mind. I don't recall the documentary going into any of that cloak and dagger stuff.

[img]http://whatculture.com/wp-content/uploads/2009/11/beautiful-mind-5939.jpg[/img]
 
Get the documentary for a much better expose of his past, with real pictures of him, his wife, etc. The movie fell far short telling us the whole picture of his life, not just the crazy part which the movie dwelled on in excess. A little disappointing. The documentary is far superior to this.....

"A Beautiful Mind" is an exceptional story, but it is only and exceptional film because of its director. Ron Howard does an amazing job of engaging his audience, introducing a brilliant main character, and making the audience experience the reality of mental illness. This could have been an unbelievable story to which very people could relate; however, the directorial mastery Howard exhibits throughout allows the audience to accompany Nash on his journey and awareness of his illness. Anyone who has been close to the frailties of the human mind will appreciate how respectfully and honestly this film approaches the subject. Howard is able to portray all the complex reactions to mental illness while maintaining the humanity and dignity of the patient. Superbly directed, wonderfully acted by Crowe and cast, this film succeeds on every level.

A harrowing and emotionally depressing movie about a genius mathematician suffering from schizophrenia. Russell Crowe presents a stunning and powerful performance as John Nash, with Jennifer Connelly as his wife Alicia. Together this strong duo represent the courage, support and love which helped Nash triumph over adversity. A biopic which follows Nash's journey of self-discovery and hardship, we first see Nash as a student in Princeton, who is struggling to find his "original idea" for his thesis. Socially isolated and being constantly ridiculed, he moves on in life when he begins to date his student, Alicia. He learns the meaning of love, but his advancement leads to a job working in government code-breaking, which soon drives him into insanity. Work soon dominates his life, along with pushing away his friends and family. He is soon informed that he is mentally ill, and that his hallucinations have made him work on a non-existent government case, with an imaginary William Parcher and Charles (his roommate). His wife Alicia manages to assist him in striving for acceptance and freedom, as he eventually "overcomes" his illness and wins the coverted Nobel Prize. One of a few movies where an actors performance really dominates and creates the film, with Crowe being seriously robbed of an Oscar. Connelly deservedly won for Best Supporting Actress, and the Best Picture was well worth it. An enthralling, captivating and thought-provoking film with kudos to Crowe and director Ron Howard ('Apollo 13').

PLOT: Biopic of the famed mathematician John Nash and his lifelong struggles with his mental health. Nash enrolled as a graduate student at Princeton in 1948 and almost immediately stood out as an odd duck. He devoted himself to finding something unique, a mathematical theorem that would be completely original. He kept to himself for the most part and while he went out for drinks with other students, he spends a lot of time with his roommate, Charles, who eventually becomes his best friend. John is soon a professor at MIT where he meets and eventually married a graduate student, Alicia. Over time however John begins to lose his grip on reality, eventually being institutionalized diagnosed with schizophrenia. As the depths of his imaginary world are revealed, Nash withdraws from society and it's not until the 1970s that he makes his first foray back into the world of academics, gradually returning to research and teaching. Last year's cult hit Memento used a creative method to show the viewer what it was like to suffer from short-term memory loss: the sequence of events was presented in reverse order, so the viewer also finds it difficult to form new memories from scene to scene. It's a great way of allowing the presentation to reflect the subject matter at hand. Ron Howard's exquisite A Beautiful Mind takes this approach one step further: it lets us into the lead character's mind. See, by the end of Memento, we're not sure what to make of Lenny as a character, but by the end of A Beautiful Mind, not only are we able to see what it's like -- if only in a superficial way -- to suffer from schizophrenia, but we also have gotten to know the brilliant mathematician John Nash, respect his hardships and deeply care about what happens to him.

Nash is played with unbridled openness by Russell Crowe in what I would call a career-making performance if Crowe wasn't already a big-time Hollywood star with several Oscar nominations (and a win last year for his passable turn in Gladiator). This is a guts-and-glory effort that is complex yet jarbled, physical and spiritual, cerebral and gentle, and everything in between. The movie opens with Nash attending Princeton University in the late 1940's as a prodigy without the discipline or guidance that could propel him to greatness. With the help of a non-social roommate named Charles (Paul Bettany), Nash learns to loosen up a bit and eventually submits a paper before end of term that would contradict Adam Smith's fundamental economic theorems. He lands a well-paying job and begins doing code-breaking work for a mysterious government figure, played by Ed Harris. Nash also steps into the teaching profession on the side, where he meets Jennifer Connelly, who, in this film, certainly makes a solid argument for teacher/student relationships. At a mathematics symposium, he is the subject of an intervention headed by a psychiatrist (Christopher Plummer). Nash is institutionalized and diagnosed with schizophrenia. From this point onward, I dare not say more.

What I will say is that, while A Beautiful Mind flirts with sentimentality and dares to overreach its grasp, it is never at the expense of the characters, who are very well drawn. Akiva Goldman's screenplay (usually more of a Joel Schumacher crony than a dramatic writer), based on Sylvia Nasar's novel, takes great care to make sure that our beliefs as viewers are attuned to what Nash himself believes. It makes for an unexpected journey at the film's two-thirds point, when both the characters and the audience are expected to temper their perceptions until they can get a handle on what to believe.

I noticed that some scenes caused people in the theatre to tsk tsk quite regularly, which started to annoy after a while. This must be a sign Ron Howard is getting it right. A brief look at his directorial list would certainly confirm he is still an artist who has produced some enriching movies. I think in this particular case, he definitely lucked out by landing Crowe. Harris, Connelly and Judd Hirsch fill their parts admirably, but this is 100% Russell's baby and he shines in every scene. Overall, in a year of sub-par films, A Beautiful Mind is certainly a beautiful find.

I finally got around to seeing this film as part of my prep-work before going to "American Gangster." I've been meaning to watch this for a while, and I was bored on a Monday night. 

So, yeah.  Not that big of a fan.

Let me explain.  The first three acts of this movie are excellent.  The fourth act, where we see the aged John Nash shambling around struggling to ignore his hallucinations and winning Nobel Prizes, is THE WORST PIECE OF CLOYING, MANIPULATIVE BULLSHIT I HAVE EVER SEEN ONSCREEN.

This movie starts out very compelling, with Russell Crowe playing John Forbes Nash Jr., a mathematical genius grad student at Princeton University.  He has a fun-loving alcoholic roommate named Charles (played to absolute perfection by Paul Bettany in the film's only consistent performance), two nerdy colleagues named Bender and Sol (played by "Rent's" Anthony Rapp, trying and failing to suppress his gay tendencies and Adam Goldberg, trying and failing to suppress his snarky Jew tendencies (you can see him pining for a smart-ass one-liner)) and a cocky, dickish rival named Hansen (played with his standard, tired cocky dickishness by Josh Lucas).  One night while out at a bar, Nash comes up with a theory on how to get laid (as far as I can tell), writes down an equation for it, and wins some kind of competition where the prize is a professorship and a side-job cracking Russian codes for the Pentagon.  
This is the mid-point of Act One.  So far, so good.  (Not so far, so great, but definitely so far, so good.) 
One of his students, Alicia, (played the radiant and excellent Jennifer Connelly) asks him out.  They begin a courtship, and these are some of the best scenes in the film. Eventually, Charles convinces Nash to propose, and they get married.
Then Ed Harris shows up as FBI Agent Parcher, enlisting Nash in some serious covert shit, complete with code number lasered into his forearm that can only be viewed under blacklight. He cracks topsecret codes that are hidden in newsprint, then drops them off in a mailbox outside a sprawling suburban mansion.  One night, as he's doing his patriotic duty, he's picked up by a frantic Parcher, who's being chased by what we can only assume are Rooskeys.  There is a high speed pursuit, the Rooskeys are killed, and Nash returns home to his worried wife, who, of course, must be kept in the dark for the sake of National Security.
So far, so implausible. But I'm still with you, movie.  The performances are so engrossing, I don't care about the gaps in logic.
Nash keeps getting crazier and crazier, until he has a nervous breakdown during a lecture and the Government comes to take him away.  Turns out (GASP!!!) Charles doesn't exist, and (SHOCKER!!!) Parcher is a figment of his imagination.  Nash is diagnosed as a paranoid schizophrenic, and subjected to ridiculously overboard shock treatement by a Gov't Shrink (played in his sleep by Christopher Plummer).
This is all well and good, but as we start seeing him talk to nobody throughout the latter half of the film, I'm wondering how fucked up you would have to be to imagine being catatonic and horizontal in the back of a speeding Ford Fairlane with a carload of KGB agents shooting at you as Ed Harris hands you a gun and screams at you to return fire.  Was that some kind of involved daydream? Talking to someone who isn't really there is one thing, but that's just ridiculous.
So now we get the obligatory human drama. He's released from the loony bin on a regimen of anti-wacky pills. But the math-addict Nash keeps working on formulas to define math stuff. Unfortunately, the anti-wacky pills are also anti-brain-worky pills. It's sad to watch this "beautiful mind" deteriorate, or at least that's what we're being force-fed by professional hack screenwriter Akiva Goldsman (he wrote "Batman & Robin" for Christ's sake). There are some nice genuine moments here: When Sol comes to visit and tells Nash that "There are more things in life than just work," and Nash replies "What are they?".  That's followed by Crowe sitting alone in the living room staring into nothingness, half-heartedly holding his infant daughter on his lap. Connelly comes into the room and grabs the child from him, startling him as he grasps at the air when she leaves.  This is the shit that Crowe is able to do with the right material, and it's breathtaking.  Unfortunately, this is the point in the script where it all falls apart.  
He's been pocketing his pills so he can continue working, but of course this means he starts hallucinating again. This time he understands that he's nuts, and with this understanding, he begs for a research position back at Princeton where his old nemesis Hansen is now the dean or something.  Turns out Hansen isn't that bad of a guy I guess, because he agrees.  Nash eventually starts teaching at Princeton again, and wins the Nobel Prize for something he did twenty-five years earlier.

This is the Fourth Act, where it all goes to shit.  Never EVER let Russell Crowe play age.  Cause he can't.  At all.  He goes from a brisk athletic walk to old-man shuffle in the span of one scene. All of a sudden he starts to sound like Foghorn Leghorn with brain damage.  The makeup just keeps getting heavier and heavier on all the characters, to the point that I literally did not recognize Connelly in the Nobel Prize scene.

The simplistic cookie cutter nature of the script is just fucking maddening.  Goldsman has Hansen challenge Nash to a game of chinese checkers or some shit in 1948 with this exchange: 
Hansen: "John.  You scared?"
Nash: "Terrified. Mortified. Stupified.  By you."

Then THIRTY FUCKING YEARS LATER, both men rememberthe exchange exactly and repeat it word for fucking word.  A simple, anachronistic, inconsequential, useless exchange is recalled EXACTLY by both men thirty years afterward?  I don't think so.  Not unless it's a cheap device in a lazy screenplay by a hack writer who needs to just Stop. Right. Now.
Oh, and even better (worse) than that: Early in the film, Judd Hirsch (yes, THAT Judd Hirsch), playing Crowe's mentor, shows him some old professor sitting in an campus tea room, and a bunch of other guys in tweed jackets come by and they each give him a fountain pen for some reason that I guess is supposed to be a sign of respect.  Then, late in the film, some Nobel representative takes Nash into the same fucking tea room to tell him he's going to win the prize, and (you guessed it) a bunch of guys come and each give him a fountain pen.  And I shit you not, Nash actually says: "That was unexpected."  
REALLY!?!?!?!?!?!?
Really, movie?
Fuck you, movie.

I was cool with everything up until the fourth act, but I can only be insulted an manipulated at the same time for so long.

The two stars are for the performances.  Everything else about the film, even Ron Howard's direction (which is usually top notch), sucked.

Oh and by the way, this is a biopic that conveniently leaves out anything that might make this guy unpalatable to a wide audience: namely that he was married several times, was involved in bisexual affairs, and was a deadbeat dad to a son that he fathered out of wedlock.

It's a bullshit movie, and absolutely did NOT deserve it's Oscars or any of the effusive praise that was heaped upon it.

This movie is primarily about his struggle and eventual reliance upon his trust in love, versus his mathematical logic.

Complete with facial ticks, mumbling, and odd hand motions, Crowe literally becomes Nash. He gives a very clear picture of a genius who is tortured by his own dementia. However, this movie has its problems. Much of the not-so-appealing facts of Nash's life was left out( child out of wedlock, the divorce and remarriage to Alicia, and accounts of reported homosexuality). What happens however when the mind works against us? When it tricks us into believing that what is not real to be the actual, destroying our sense of being? This is what ?A Beautiful Mind? tackles, a thought-provoking film based on a true story with lots of brain behind it, but more importantly, lots of heart within it.

Russell Crowe is John Nash, a mathematical genius who sees life through numbers. We curiously watch him as he observes a pack of pigeons and tries to formulate an algorithm for their feeding patterns; or when John witnesses a mugging, and he sets up the incident as vectors and summarizing the event through complicated theorems and formulas. John basically wants to explain life?s behaviors through precise mathematical proofs, but his own behavior is somewhat enigmatic itself.

He is a bit of a loner, an anti-social scholar at Princeton University, scribbling equations on chalkboards and windows that only 0.001% of us will understand. Social interactions are not quite honed, as he tries to get a girl to go out with him, but the few words that he does say includes something about exchanging bodily fluids. In time however, John forms a few good friends, and even manages to have a girl, Alicia (Jennifer Connelly) fall for him.

[Warning: Plot spoiler in next paragraph]

The film is set in the 1940?s, and the Cold War seedling is burgeoning. Mathematicians made the Allied victory possible, and their help is sought ought once more to help against the Russians. John has a knack for breaking cryptic codes and is hired by the government to interpret intercepted numerical messages sent by the enemy. He is involved in highly classified projects and has basically been transformed into a spy. However, the situation gets a bit gnarly as men in dark trench coats and fedoras begin to chase John. On top of that, it doesn?t quite help that he suffers from schizophrenia, a degenerative brain condition that causes John to hallucinate and slowly lose contact with reality. He must now depend on his human connections to help him get through the dilemma.

?A Beautiful Mind? is a love story, a biography and a spy flick wrapped up together in one package, and works quite effectively on all these levels. Written by Akiva Goldsman and Sylvia Nasar, along with the highly taut direction of Ron Howard, the film is tremendously engaging, despite running a bit too long. It has surprises that will keep you guessing, but most of all, it evokes drama that is heartfelt. Anchored by the strong chemistry between John and Alicia, his personal troubles sifting nightmares from reality becomes a powerful human struggle. A man who achieved greatness all by himself now needs the assistance of others to get through life.

The performances are reliably excellent from its two leading stars. ?A Beautiful Mind? is getting a lot of clout for the Oscars with its multiple Golden Globe nominations, which might mean another nomination for Russell Crowe for Best Actor (which he won for ?Gladiator? and NOT ?The Insider??still quite upsetting). Crowe is great as John Nash, although sometimes he looks a tad bit old for the part. The beautiful Jennifer Connelly is wonderful too as John?s love interest, and boy does she know how to pick a good script. Directed by
Ron Howard
At Princeton University, John Nash struggles to make a worthwhile contribution to serve as his legacy to the world of mathematics. He finally makes a revolutionary breakthrough that will eventually earn him the Nobel Prize. After graduate school he turns to teaching, becoming romantically involved with his student Alicia. Meanwhile the government asks his help with breaking Soviet codes, which soon gets him involved in a terrifying conspiracy plot. Nash grows more and more paranoid until a discovery that turns his entire world upside down. Now it is only with Alicia's help that he will be able to recover his mental strength and regain his status as the great mathematician we know him as today.

"A Beautiful Mind", based on the novel by Sylvia Nasar, is the story of John Forbes Nash Jr., the genius mathematician, whose life suddenly takes a turn for the worse when he is diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia. After fierce battles with his inner self, he overcomes this and returns to win the Nobel Prize in 1994 for his brakethrough game theory in economics that he had been working on during his years in Princeton University in the 1950s.
As a movie, "A Beautiful Mind" is absolutely great (It is so much more, but I cannot find the words to praise it enough, so I will simply go with "great" =). Not only does it have a strong point and an importaint message to the viewer, but it delivers it in a touching and sensitive, partly even humourous kind of way, with the help of powerful actors, a great screenplay and even a few special effects to boost it up. So for anyone whose grown tired of the consant pointless action-movies out there, and instead want to immerse themselves into a character-driven story that might actually bring a tear to your eyes.

Russell Crowe is one of the best actors in the industry and he proves this through his role of the Nobel prize winning economist, John Nash, in A Beautiful Mind, an amazing movie, possibly the best one by Ron Howard, who unfortunately directed the crap known as The Da Vinci Code. It touches on a very original and different subject and according to my phsychology teacher, this movie probably has one of the most accurate representations of schizophrenia in the media. It was sad for the most part, with a few comic scenes here and there. The acting was wonderful; all the stars played their parts perfectly.  However, good the movie may be, it wasn't perfect. The first half was slightly confusing and it was hard to see which direction this movie was going to. However, after the truth is revealed about John's illness, things begin to piece together and we can understand it much better, but here's where the second problem comes. The second part gets somewhat boring as it's quite a slow movie. However, if one take the time to watch this movie and not get all fussy about it being slow...for sure, they will enjoy a great movie, which is worth every penny you spend on it.

I wasn't actually planning on going to see "A Beautiful Mind" in the first place, but as it was, I was convinced by the friend that accompanied me that it was truly something to see. And now, after seeing it, I thank her for that. Instead of spending two and a half hours watching George Clooney and Matt Damon rob casinos or Kevin Spacey and Julianne Moore dealing with their problems in New Foundland, I found myself pulled into another kind of story, a powerful, emotional story of how one man learned to battle his own demons and dazzle the world.

"A Beautiful Mind", based on the novel by Sylvia Nasar, is the story of John Forbes Nash Jr., the genius mathematician, whose life suddenly takes a turn for the worse when he is diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia. After fierce battles with his inner self, he overcomes this and returns to win the Nobel Prize in 1994 for his brakethrough game theory in economics that he had been working on during his years in Princeton University in the 1950s.

John Nash, portrayed very well by the versatile and brilliant Russell Crowe, is a partly shy, yet ironic and sometimes even arrogant, gifted young student studying in Princeton University in the late 1940s. He dedicates his time to numbers and equations, set on to solving every problem at hand, rather than mingling with co-students on the football field or in the pub.

Nash is later on introduced to Sylvia (played by the lovely Jennifer Connely), a physics student attending his classes. She helps Nash to open up and eventually discover love.

Enter William Parcher (played by Ed Harris), a shadowy and mysterious agent working for the Department of Defense. Parcher, after realizing Nash's ability to see mathematical and geometrical patterns everywhere, approaches Nash with a mission that involves national security.

Now, amidst his work and relationship, Nash is suddenly thrown into a whirlwind of emotions and disbeliefs as he is diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia. And this is the part where "A Beautiful Mind" truly shines: in portraying the disorder from Nash's own point of view. In a powerful and emotional way, it shows the viewer how difficult an illness like this can be to not only face, but overcome, something that people today may not always realize.

Before seeing this movie, I must admit that I was a bit afraid that casting such a well-known actor as Russell Crowe as the main character would ruin the image of John Nash, forcing the viewer to see Crowe, rather than Nash. This is a common problem when dealing with famous actors, but to my surprise, it didn't much bother me much. And the same goes for Ed Harris.

As a movie, "A Beautiful Mind" is absolutely great (It is so much more, but I cannot find the words to praise it enough, so I will simply go with "great" =). Not only does it have a strong point and an importaint message to the viewer, but it delivers it in a touching and sensitive, partly even humourous kind of way, with the help of powerful actors, a great screenplay and even a few special effects to boost it up. So for anyone whose grown tired of the consant pointless action-movies out there, and instead want to immerse themselves into a character-driven story that might actually bring a tear to your eyes, I sincerily recommend "A Beautiful Mind".

Though I knew something about the movie before watching it I wasn't expecting Nash was that mentally ill. I was happy that the movie didn't end here. Unlike The Sixth Sense, where the movie ends once the main character finds out what was going on, this movie continues and shows how Nash and his family and friends dealt with this illness. A Beautiful Mind
2001
Drama
Rated: PG-13
Running Time: 135 minutes
Starring: Russell Crowe, Jennifer Connelly, Ed Harris, Paul Bettany, Josh Lucas, Adam Goldberg
Directed By: Ron Howard
Rating: 8 out of 10
Outline
A genius breaking government codes has his life turned upside down when all that is might not really be.
Review
Beautifully directed and even more so beautifully acted this film will take you down a road of intellectual insightfulness. Director Ron Howard has the uncanny ability of keeping you on the edge of your seat the whole movie and then blowing you away with heart wrenching finishes. Russell Crowe turns in an Oscar worthy performance as mentally unstable John Nash. A genius with social ineptness who goes through life with only his lack of success as his main enemy. After a major break through using math that would later be globally acknowledged he takes on a government job breaking soviet codes. His life seems perfect after marrying the love of his life Alicia brilliantly played by Jennifer Connelly. It is perfect that is until paranoia sets in and he feels like he is being watched where ever he goes. This movie takes you on a mind trip as much as one as John Nash is suffering. You do not know if he is delusional or telling the truth. His world is shattered as he deals with the conspiracy of soviets wanting him dead. The years of struggle as John copes with his mental instability are amazing to go through. The movie starts off dreadfully slow but if you can sit through it you will be rewarded with an incredibly thoughtful film one that will make you cry many times over. The supporting cast of perennial favorites Ed Harris and Paul Bettany lends to the awesome star power of this film. The movie has a very quiet musical score that is thoughtful and caring. Not the easiest film to watch as the topic will leave some depressed and others bored it is one that I feel everyone should watch as it has a great message of overcoming ones demons. That and the fact it will make you feel about every emotion in the book which truly is the mark of a great drama. Watching Crowe on screen will mesmerize you as his mannerisms, voice and demeanor are all very well put together. He seems very cognizant of the fact people are watching him yet he brushes it off well and just works his magic. People who like hardcore dramas will like this more then the average film watcher but I do give it a huge recommendation. If you can sit through the dull parts it is a road well worth the travel.

O fenómeno dos óscares tem na indústria cinematográfica efeitos realmente positivos e promocionais. Pode ter, no entanto consequências nefastas, em parte, impostas pelo peso da `tradição`. Este ano o cinema norte americano, não teve, salvo pontualíssimas excepções, à altura das constantes expectativas inerentes à maior fábrica de sonhos do mundo. Para tal efeito terá ainda contribuído, muito recentemente, os acontecimentos do 11 de Setembro. Quando se pensava que tal tragédia poderia ser sintetizada em algo muito agradável, projeccionando um cinema mais reflexivo, e ao mesmo tempo, reflectindo uma abordagem mais profunda e desprendida em termos emocionais e até psico sociais, eis que deparamos com uma `depuração` (e digo-o sem querer parecer conspirativo ou paranóico) da já de si tendencialmente `alva`, indústria norte americana da sétima arte. 
Tudo isto para referir que a obra: `A beautiful mind` é um melodrama encomendado. Isto soa a lugar comum, em vésperas de óscares, mas contudo, penso não ser justo dissociar a realidade que medeia a obra do seu mais ou menos questionável conteúdo. Não quero com isto retirar o mérito intrínseco que eventualmente possa vir a possuir o filme em face da sua qualidade cinematográfica. 
O ser humano sente necessidade de constante aperfeiçoamento e de modelos inspiradores e o cinema preenche essa necessidade. Pode faze-lo de forma mais descarada (embora não necessariamente negativa) ou pode gizar essa vontade através de meras nuances (também necessariamente mais ou menos inspirados). O que se passa em `Beautiful Mind` traduz uma tendência recente do cinema, enquanto veículo modelador de consciências, de levar a cabo uma tarefa de auto preservação dos certos valores humanos quando confrontados com a dor e o sofrimento. 
Saímos do cinema, após este filme, convencidos de que John Nash Jr., genial matemático norte americano, é um herói. O problema centra-se precisamente neste ponto. Não queiramos confundir em primeiro lugar a personagem com o homem e depois a genialidade com a sua capacidade de sofrimento. Haverá muito boa gente que por admirar o homem e seus feitos, louva o filme. É, na realidade pelo facto desta obra ser um exercício de manipulação descarada, que temos dificuldade, no meio da toda a sua excelência intelectual e esquizofrenia compulsiva, de encontrar e homenagear John Nash Jr. ? o homem. 
Várias vozes se fizeram valer acerca de Ron Howard ser o homem ideal para levar a cabo esta produção. Não podia estar mais de acordo na medida em que se conhece a sua anterior obra. Howard tem sido até então, um realizador competente, um virtuoso da sétima arte, mas não uma `beautiful mind` do mesmo. Desde cedo assistimos a determinadas visões que não destoavam do panorama cinematográfico de então, sendo que a imagética recente tem demonstrado cada vez mais apetência por este `género` (se é que poderá ser considerado um...) de `fast cinema`. Determinada dimensão onírica onde se quer desesperadamente mostrar, mostrar por vezes seja o que for. Ora, Howard tem sido exímio em criar atmosferas agradáveis e fantásticas (mas sempre para menores de 18 anos, em atmosfera familiar, diria mesmo) e em se ausentar das decisões de fundo que se exigem aos maiores nomes de sétima arte (e `decisões` não necessita aqui de ser um termo com grande densidade...). Veja-se `The Grinch`, `Parenthood` ou `Edtv`. Já tentou subir à `primeira liga` do cinema, com `Backdraft` ou `Apolo 13`, mas sempre com um certo cunho de superficialidade e de propensão para o moralismo exasperante. Por muito que me custe admiti-lo à terceira não foi de vez. Volta a incair no mesmo erro, embora desta vez com a atenuante do argumento ser tendencialmente mais simples, em irónico contraste com a complexidade do tema central: a adversidade. Por outras palavras, este era um realizador ideal. Prata da casa, capaz de traduzir visualmente, de forma competente, uma história comprometida e superficial, sem agitar demasiadamente as águas. Howard põe o dedo na ferida, mas seguramente não nas feridas certas. 
Esta biopic sobre o génio matemático norte americano, John Nash Jr., galardoado com um nóbel em 1994, é uma reflexão `sentimentalona`, acerca da genialidade e da esquizofrenia. A obra contém, inegavelmente, momentos de bom cinema, particularmente quando nos é revelada a dimensão genial de Nash. Acessos de fruição criativa perfeitamente inesperados e acima de tudo uma misantropia, que é um dos `what if...` mais interessantes do filme, são disso bons exemplos. Já Nash ? esquizofrénico, claudica rotundamente. Confesso que era um terreno propenso a clichets e isso a espaços aconteceu. Esgazeado e confuso, Nash vai progressivamente envolvendo-se e envolvendo todos, na densa teia de pensamentos que funde a realidade e a fantasia. Mas note-se que isso nós só sabemos quando Howard bem entende. Eurico de Barros chama a isto desonestidade e eu não poderia estar mais de acordo. Acrescentando talvez falta de perspicácia visual. Howard não captou de forma conveniente a herança de Linch, ou mesmo nas lições do `novato` David Fincher, traduzindo uma certa dimensão psicológica de Nash num sádico exercício de manipulação. A total desinformação do espectador que não consegue acompanhar a bipartição do universo de Nash, ou a tensão entre o visível e o invisível, não é justa. 
É na relação com o outro e numa certa exclusão demencial que residem os elementos que mereceriam um maior aprofundamento. A tradução do caldeirão emotivo e intelectual no interior do qual Nash, age e reage, com total desinteresse por quase tudo o que o rodeia  (excepto a inesperada percepção de que tem que efectivar um relacionamento sério com `alguém` do sexo oposto; é curioso observar que é Alicia que progressivamente se apaixona por Nash, deixando este, que alguém o ame, mais por necessidade de normalidade social do que por qualquer outra razão; aliás o amor só nasce mais tarde muito provavelmente sob a forma de reconhecimento após o calvário da sua doença: até então tudo se passara com imensa admiração mútua) é dado pelo olhar maravilhoso de Russel Crowe. 
Crowe é incontestavelmente um actor brilhante aliando performances mais físicas a outras de maior vertente psicológica. E surpreendentemente ou não tem-se saído bem em quase todas elas. Na obra, atente-se que nunca tinha Ron Howard dado tanta importância à direcção dos seus actores. Talvez essa seja uma razão que contribua para que a interpretação seja, em meu entender, o ponto mais alto do filme. Russel Crowe, enquanto epicentro da narrativa, tem naturalmente o papel mais preponderante (embora este raciocínio na verdade nem sempre bata certo). Em parte pelo interesse nos últimos anos prestado pela academia norte americana, por interpretações de personagens diminuídas ou excluídas de uma ou outra forma (veja-se Dustin Hoffman em `Rain Man` Nicholas Cage em `Leaving Las Vegas` ou mais recentemente Geoffrey Rush no emblemático `Shine`), nota-se em Crowe a preocupação em limar arestas no seu papel, para mais facilmente caminhar para o óscar. Deliciosa é a forma pela qual Crowe nos transmite austeridade, experiência e maturidade (como se revela na sequência da entrega dos óscares) e como já nos tinha sido evidenciado em `The Insider`. Já mais discutível é Nash enquanto jovem. Inseguro, nervoso e titubiante, suspeitamos, a espaços, de um certo ?over acting? naturalmente desnecessário. Tal como o filme também a interpretação ascende progressivamente. 
Há sim que realçar no campo interpretativo Jennifer Connely, jovem actriz, bastante talentosa que tem vindo como poucas a gerir a sua carreira. Desde `Dark City`, passando por `Requiem for a Dream` ou `Pollock` tem nos habituado a boas presenças no ecrã. Desta vez não foge à regra. Jennifer é no fundo a estabilidade por contraposição a certa indefinição constante de Nash. Assim sendo é ela que lhe dá a mão, ajudando-o a sair de um `problem with no solution`. É ela a trave mestra do frágil edifício emocional de Nash. E que força ela lhes/nos transmite. Quem se lembrará de Emily Watson em `Angela?s Ashes`? Há ainda que salientar a sub aproveitamento do talento de Ed Harris nesta obra. Tem uma intervenção menor, numa personagem pouco desenvolvida. 
Queria apenas ainda fazer referência à realização que considero competente, mas sem rasgos de genialidade, daí a nomeação só se conceber na prática corrente de distribuir nomeações `aos molhos` a cada filme e não privilegiando com rigor e isenção, cada categoria de per se. Curioso ainda a nomeação para a montagem que acho extremamente injusto. Um dos sinais reveladores do que falo é que este foi um dos poucas obras rodadas por ordem cronológica... Se bem que não decisivo, ilustrará que o trabalho de montagem não é efectivamente merecedor de distinção. 
Para terminar (dado que já me alonguei o bastante) queria apenas dizer que o argumento é um dos pontos sintomáticos de toda a obra e que evidencia que `A beautiful mind` é no fundo um `feel good movie` a puxar ao sentimentalismo. Ter-se-á pensado que convinha subtrair certos elementos à história, como é o caso da sua mais que provável bissexualidade (existindo apenas uma ténue e duvidosa alusão a tal através do companheiro de quarto de Nash),ou o filho que teve de outro relacionamento. Ninguém põe em causa que o cinema tem que gerir o seu tempo, por definição finito, de uma maneira que por vezes suscita discordância. Também ninguém questiona que se trata de uma adaptação livre e de uma pura obra de ficção (para usar a acepção mais rigorosa da palavra). O que se critica não é a necessidade de fazer uma opção, mas sim aquela que foi feita em particular. Quero crer que enquanto exercício narrativo a obra cai numa certa repetitividade de fórmulas e enquanto homenagem a Nash assaca-se-lhe uma despropositada falta de isenção. 
Em resumo, Nash é nesta obra um tanto ou quanto instrumentalizado. Serve os Estados Unidos, nação actualmente com a auto estima em baixo, através de mais um dos inúmeros episódios de exaltação de grandes heróis americanos... 
Esperemos nós que `Ali` não seja um dos próximos capítulos.

A Beautiful Mind (2001) -- [7.5] -- Russell Crowe and Jennifer Connelly are at the top of their game in "A Beautiful Mind," Ron Howard's Oscar-winning biopic about John Nash, the brilliant but haunted mathematician who overcame schizophrenia and received the Nobel Prize. These are the best performances I've seen from Crowe and Connelly -- their relationship is the glue that holds the film together. The first two-thirds of the movie is an engaging psychological thriller -- the less you know about the story, the better it will surprise you. Unfortunately, the film devolves into a sentimental drama in the final thirty minutes, but the pros outweigh the cons overall. In addition to the best picture Oscar, the film also won for directing and adapted screenplay. Crowe was nominated for his performance and Connelly took home the trophy for best supporting actress.

"A Beautiful Mind" tells a fairly biographical tale of professor John Nash (Russel Crowe), a winner of a Nobel prize. We first meet him as a student at Princeton - he's fairly charming, but ultimately unlikable due to his facade of pretentious dialect and obsession with his studies. Although a genius mathematically, it's very clear that this is a man void of social skills. Years later, the film takes an unexpected twist at the arrival of William Parcher (Ed Harris), a government agent that we don't get to know a whole lot about. At the same time, he marries Alicia (Jennifer Connelly), and soon has a son with her. 

However, eventually John's world comes crashing down when he's told that his code-breaking work for the government agent is all fake - he's simply imagined all of it. Not only that, he imagined one of his best friends through college, Charles (Paul Bettany). The film shifts it's focus to Alicia, who has to struggle with the fact that her husband is schizophrenic and potentially dangerous. It's no longer the story of a broken man who lost everything - it's a story of the wife who has to cope with it. 

Not knowing anything about John Nash before watching this film, I really had no idea what I was in for. Needless to say, I was pleasantly surprised. My eyes were rolling at this "top secret government agency" work, so it certainly made quite a bit of sense when it was all an illusion. I was thinking it was just lousy storytelling! That being said, one could argue that it took too long for the true story to be revealed. I was fairly uninterested with everything that happened before the mental institution. I do understand why they did it, however, as it made us feel for John Nash and know who he is as a person, rather then immediately introducing us to "some crazy guy".

Ron Howard's direction is very good. Besides all the "code-breaking" effects that everyone was talking about when the film was released, there's a lot of really neat and innovative decisions. Perhaps my favorite was a car chase scene involving the "Russians" trying to kill John and William. The sound of the cars is almost muted, while the wonderful score gets a chance to illuminate and it's accented by gunshots. It was so relieving to see a car chase that was something more than noisy and obnoxious. It was beautiful as a chaotic mess - something I wish more directors would do. Very cool stuff.

Russel Crowe has never been an actor i've been completely sold on. I can't deny his talents, but he seems to have the same delivery and character in just about everything i've seen him in. He seemed to be void of any range. Well, he definitely won me over in this. As a delusional man, he was completely believable... and, he was equally as believable and charming as a young student. This was a role that allowed him to showcase his range as an actor and it's really a very memorable performance. Jennifer Connelly is also very good and plays off of him well.

This would've been almost perfect, but I didn't like the melodramatic mess it turned into at the end. I know this is a movie about a man receiving the Nobel peace prize, but it just seemed so transparent. This was a complex film all the way through, and at the end it turns into a shallow crowd pleaser. It lost me emotionally when I was supposed to be the most touched. I also hated the scenes where John is "ignoring" his hallucinations... such as the scene where he didn't hug the little girl. Although well acted, the concept seemed so cheesy and simple. That being said, this is still a great film. It has it's downfalls, but there's a whole lot going for it that more than make up for them. I enjoyed it very much.

Keep in the back of your mind that this a feel-good drama-- one should expect nothing more and nothing less from the director of Splash, Coccoon and Willow-- and you should be well equipped to enjoy this film. The perennially amazing Russel Crowe stars as John Nash, a man who taught us to look at the world as a system (a "game") but whose biggest challenge was not an equation, but conquering his own brilliant "beautiful" mind. Jennifer Connelly, gorgeous and amazing expressive as usual, plays his wife with a tragic dignity and loyalty (Nash and his wife did not stay together in real life, I believe, but Howard loves his faithful housewife characters.) The cast is rounded out by Paul Bettany, the regal and mature Christopher Plummer, Judd Hirsch (who just can't get enough mathematician roles) a terrifying Ed Harris, and Rent alumnus Anthony Rapp, all under the workable direction of Howard and a gorgeous score by James Horner

Nel 1949, il ventunenne e talentuoso matematico John Nash entra nella prestigiosa Università di Princeton con una borsa di studio per il dottorato. Refrattario ad instaurare rapporti sociali, Nash ha solo due amici: Charles, il suo compagno di stanza, e le formule matematiche. Ossessionato dal pensiero di trovare un'idea originale a cui applicare le sue formule, John riesce nel suo obiettivo: in una tesi di dottorato di sole 27 pagine espone geniali intuizioni fondamentali allo sviluppo della "Teoria dei Giochi", facendo così diventare obsolete le teorie economiche di Adam Smith.

Le sue idee gli procurano fama e un importante posto di ricercatore al MIT di Boston, dove conferma la sua intelligenza matematica. In piena "guerra fredda" viene contattato dall'esercito per la sua incredibile capacità di decodificatore. Entra così in contatto con l'"eminenza grigia" William Parcher, oscuro personaggio del governo che lo assolda per una missione top secret. Contemporaneamente John trova anche l'amore di Alicia, una giovane studentessa di fisica, che diventa sua moglie.

La vita di Nash viene a questo punto sconvolta da una terribile scoperta. Charles, la sua nipotina e lo stesso Parcher sono in realtà solo proiezioni della mente malata di Nash, affetto da una grave forma di schizofrenia. Vagando come un fantasma tra cliniche e manicomi viene sottoposto a numerose sedute di shock insulinico e ad una massiccia dose di farmaci. Grazie all'affetto ed alla vicinanza dei familiari, Alicia in particolare, e alla sua forza mentale riesce ad ignorare le sue allucinazioni, e a convivere sia pure con sofferenza con la malattia, tornando anche all'attività accademica. Infatti, Nash diventa docente a Princeton, e nel 1994 è insignito del Premio Nobel per l'economia. La difficile ma riuscita convivenza di Nash con la sua malattia è simboleggiata dalla visione dei suoi tre fantasmi uno accanto all'altro che lo osservano dopo la cerimonia di premiazione.[it.wikipedia.org]

Russell Crowe plays the part of John Nash almost flawlessly. From a struggling genius, to a schizophrenic, to a loving husband, Crowe plays his roles as a fidgety prodigy at Princeton excellently. John Nash's wife, whom he met while lecturing at the university, is portrayed by Jennifer Conelly. The movie is based on the life of the famous John Nash, the creator of the Nash Equillibrium and other theories and equations. It portrays how a young genius struggling with schizophrenia overcame the dreaded disease to become a respected man in the mathematical world. The movie starts off with young John Nash at his first day in Princeton, and meeting his 'roommate', whom he would later discover was only part of his imagination. In between the lines of his effort to deal with schizophrenia and depression, therein lies a beautiful love story of John Nash and his wife, Alicia. The characters of the story are portrayed so beautifully by the actors that one can feel their inner struggle and emotions. It is a touching story of love and dreams, and helps viewers understand the often misunderstood disease called schizophrenia. All in all, this movie was a very refreshing watch and is my all time favorite.
