Russell Crowe wonderfully portrays the brilliant mathematician John Nash in this beautiful film from director Ron Howard. Jennifer Connelly plays his devoted wife, and everyone involved delivers great performances. Oscar-winner for Best Picture 2001.

The presence of Russell Crowe dominates the movie, and I think his portrayal of John Nash is the film's biggest asset. Jennifer Connelly is also quite good as Nash's loving and supportive wife-my only complaint is that I wish her role had been bigger and more complex. I liked the performances of the actors in the other supporting roles as well, particularly Ed Harris, who plays a mysterious U.S. government undercover agent. There are two things that director Ron Howard and screenwriter Akiva Goldsman did in the film that I really admire. One is the way they found to show the audience the delusions and paranoia suffered by a schizophrenic. The other is how they were able to illustrate the essence of Nash's Nobel-winning mathematical idea in terms of guys trying to pick up girls in a bar.

A Beautiful Mind is a beautifully written, effectively acted, and meticulously crafted effort that is likely to remind many viewers of a simple axiom: a movie doesn't have to be groundbreaking to be compelling. Originality is a prized commodity because there is so little of it in Hollywood these days, but, when filmmakers do such a skillful job with familiar elements, their efforts should be acknowledged. Affecting without being overtly manipulative, A Beautiful Mind tells the life story of John Nash, a Nobel prize winner who struggled through most of his adult life with schizophrenia. As directed by Ron Howard, this becomes a tale not only of one man's battle to overcome his own disability, but of the overreaching power of love - a theme that has been embraced by films as diverse as It's a Wonderful Life and Rocky.

A Beautiful Mind may have been developed to be a crowd-pleaser as well as a tear-jerker, but genuine craft is evident in the way the pieces were assembled. The movie never becomes cloying, nor does it threaten to drown us beneath an outpouring of false sentiment. This is no Patch Adams, filled with saccharine-coated artificiality. The characters are effectively drawn and their plight touches an emotional chord. A Beautiful Mind offers a catharsis without insulting the intelligence. Sadly, too few movies these days can make a similar claim. This film argues that there are still instances when Hollywood-produced, big budget movies are worth a viewer's investment of time and money.

A Beautiful Mind purports to tell the true story of Professor John Nash (Russell Crowe), but, while the gross facts may be accurate, one must expect embellishment of the details. Narrative features are not constrained by the same rules that limit documentaries. We first meet Nash as a student at Princeton in 1947. He is brilliant but erratic - a mathematical genius who lacks social skills. He is aided in making it through those difficult years by his roommate, Charles (Paul Bettany). Years later, following an astounding breakthrough that revolutionizes economics, John is teaching at M.I.T. and doing code-breaking work for a shady government agent, William Parcher (Ed Harris). It's at this time that John meets, falls in love with, and marries Alicia (Jennifer Connelly). But his happy world soon starts to crumble. John is afflicted with paranoid hallucinations; by the time he is taken to a mental hospital under the care of the mysterious Dr. Rosen (Christopher Plummer), he is diagnosed as having an advanced case of schizophrenia.

For Russell Crowe, the winner of last year's Best Actor Oscar, this is another opportunity to broaden his range. Crowe successfully buries his personality beneath Nash's, allowing the character to come to the fore (a necessity, considering the actor's current load of off-screen baggage). Much as he did in The Insider, Crowe shows no difficulty inhabiting the skin of a real-life individual who has a stronger intellect than physique. And, when it comes to the sequences depicting Nash battling his demons, Crowe's performance is utterly convincing. Meanwhile, Jennifer Connelly is luminous as Alicia. Although the showier performance belongs to Crowe, it is Connelly's complex work, depicting a woman torn by love for and fear of the same man, that elevates the film to a higher level. The actress was unjustly overlooked for Requiem for a Dream; hopefully, the Academy will not repeat that mistake. Solid support is provided by Ed Harris and Christopher Plummer.

A viewer certainly doesn't have to be a mathematical expert to appreciate what A Beautiful Mind offers, although those with a strong left-brain component may relate better to John Nash than right-brainers. The movie tosses mathematical theories and theorems in the audience's direction, but explains them simply and lucidly; no one is going to become lost or bored. A Beautiful Mind isn't about mathematics except as a symbol. It's about human frailty and the ability to triumph over it. Nash could just as easily be a doctor, a lawyer, or a construction worker and the essence of the story would not change.

The strength of the writing and production values elevate A Beautiful Mind far above "disease of the week movie" quality. At the core of the picture lies the relationship between John and Alicia, and the tribulations that the strength of their bond allows them to overcome. On one occasion, a friend asks Alicia how she can continue to stay with her stricken husband, and she replies with a succinct explanation that everyone who has ever been in love will understand. A Beautiful Mind defies the conventional Hollywood wisdom that love is passion and romance. For John and Alicia, it is painful, heartbreaking work. And, while hearts and flowers are great for a fantasy, this is the kind of expression of emotion that touches a deeper chord.

John Nash goes through a myriad of highs and lows from his time as a Mathematics student in graduate school at Princeton in the late 1940's to his Nobel Prize win for Economics in 1994. A brilliant but somewhat arrogant and antisocial man, Nash preferred to spend his time with his thoughts, which were primarily of seeing mathematical formula associated with everyday occurrences, than with people. Two people he did make a connection with were Charles, his roommate at Princeton, and Alicia Larde, one of his students when he was teaching at M.I.T. in the early 1950's. He and Alicia eventually marry. As time goes on, Nash lives more and more within himself which causes major problems in his life. But Alicia stands by her husband to his redemption to the Nobel Prize win. Nash learns that his graduate school colleagues, with whom he had a cordial but somewhat distant relationship, are closer friends than he imagined, although in his later life he really does miss Charles' company more than anything despite knowing that spending time with Charles is not in his or anyone's best interest.

I've searched high and low through multiple viewings of A Beautiful Mind, trying to find something redeeming, something that makes this film worthy of such accolades, and I still can't find it. Mostly it induces cringes. I've never understood the extreme tolerance of Connelly's Alicia to the bluntly boorish behavior of Crowe's John Nash, with no justification that we can see, particularly early in their relationship, when most sane people would give up. Is she just a glutton for punishment? Sure, he looks great in a t-shirt, but come on. The relationship between the real Nash and his wife apparently bears little resemblance to what we get here -- she was not the slavishly devoted spouse Goldsman wants us to think she was -- and maybe that's what prompts Connelly's screaming fit in one particularly awful scene: she's just frustrated by the impossibility of portraying the impossibly saintly woman she's being asked to portray.

Though it's just as easy to blame Howard for letting Connelly's tantrum end up on film. He has rarely met a piece of over- the- topness he didn't like. The action-movie glee with which Howard depicts some of Nash's delusions don't even make sense -- how does a schizophrenic imagine himself involved in a car chase? Nash's delusions are otherwise shown to have some believable basis in his own reality, a sort of plausible deniability -- the imaginary best friend always has some excuse for not meeting Alicia, for instance -- so what's the deal with the car chase? Is Nash driving his own car alone, and if so, how does he explain to himself the next day why his windows aren't shot out like they were in his paranoid fantasy? Is he just sitting on the ground somewhere dreaming, and if so, what does he think when he wake up to reality again? To make us understand how these kinds of delusions fit into Nash's mindscape would be to let us in on the secret, and Goldsman and Howard aren't interested in doing that just yet, at this point in the film. They're more interested in fudging the boundaries between reality and delusion, in cheating the audience in order to "surprise" us later than they are in giving us any real insight into Nash's illness or Nash's character. Tricksy filmmakers -- we hates them.

The best line -- though unintentionally so -- in the film comes early on, when Nash talks of a former teacher of his who described him as having been "born with two helpings of brain but only half a helping of heart." Just like Howard's Grinch! What a spoilsport Nash is to all the Whos of Princeton, stealing their thunder and winning a Nobel Prize, all while having a heart two sizes too small. Ah, but he has a beautiful mind. I'm not quite sure what that means, but it sounds nice, doesn't it? Like nice, smooth, bland pap.

Gorgeous, wonderful movie.  While not a deep look into what it's like to have a chronic, severe mental illness (usually classified as Schizophrenia and/or Bipolar Disorder), it does acknowledge something that most people with either of these two disorders are well aware: there is a fine line between genius and madness, and this movie accentuates that brilliantly.  It poses the question of, "Would Nash have been quite as brilliant and unique, had he not been Schizophrenic?"  Unlikely - the mind does some fascinating things when it's not quite 'perfect'.  Even when he was not actively battling/ignoring his delusions, he still perceived life quite differently from those around him (ie. his early comments re Adam Smith's economic theory.)  This is a beautiful depiction of mental illness, in that it shows that mental illness isn't *always* the all-encompassing phenomena that Hollywood often likes to show it as - people with mental illness do often have jobs, marriages, etc.  They also have bouts of madness to deal with.  It's the way they weave these two together that makes this film so worthwhile.

A skillful adaptation of a real-life story by director Ron Howard, who matures beyond the facile emotions and obviousness inherent to most of his previous work, embracing a new level of maturity that is a welcome compliment to his clear, if workmanlike visual style. Howard has always been a reliable film craftsman, efficiently translating words into pictures even if his compositions have remained more functional than creative. It's a curse endemic to those who made their bones in television, including Howard's contemporaries Garry Marshall and Penny Marshall. Despite two successful decades on the A-list, they have few major-league peers with such a lack of distinguishable artistic signatures. Without skipping a beat, Howard has moved effortlessly from the rapid-fire compactness of Apollo 13 (1995) to the bloated, sugary, over-the-top razzle-dazzle of the almost unforgivably heinous How the Grinch Stole Christmas (2000). So equated is he with a glossy, marketable broadness that the sheer elegance and subtlety of his approach to this largely internal story is astonishing. It's a quantum leap forward that would be comparable to the achievement of Steven Spielberg with Schindler's List (1995), if not for the difference in emotional, physical, and historical scale. Always a demanding, exacting actor, Russell Crowe continues a winning streak by delivering the latest in a series of knockout performances, adroitly handled by a director who seems simpatico with his every choice. The film's structural gimmick turns in on itself halfway through, challenging the viewer to observe every previous and subsequent event through the eyes of paranoia, a brilliant twist that works beautifully, even better so because it is never hammered indelicately home by the filmmaker. A Beautiful Mind (2001) is a serious, fully realized story gracefully handled by Howard, proving that an artist never stops evolving no matter how accomplished his resumÃ©.

I've stated before that this film always felt a bit overrated to me, and while I stand by that, don't let that be misleading;  it is a great film, I just question those who exalt it to the level of one of the greatest films ever made.  The story of John Nash and his battles to make true breakthroughs in the field of mathematics while battling schizophrenia was fascinating and highly uplifting at several moments.  But the tone of the film reminded me of so many other films of this sort where a character must overcome their personal flaws in order to triumph, and while I won't assail the film for that as there are many classic pictures that use this plot point, I did feel like much of the style, acting, and structure of this film seemed all-too-familiar.  The film is primarily driven by the performances from Crowe and Connelly;  the scenes of Crow in the throes of his illness and Connelly struggling to care and nurture for a man she doesn't fully recognize encompassed what I felt was the strongest part of the film.  I also love the opening, where Crowe feels like a freakish figure because of his unorthodox behavior to those around him, and yet he is likely the smartest of the men around him.  Though the praise on this film is a little excessive, it is definitely quality viewing, and I will absolutely agree it is a movie you can feel comfortable cheering for.

A Beautiful Mind is aesthetic and believable. Starring Russel Crowe as John Nash, the film follows Nash's growth in intelligence and his deterioration in emotion as schizophrenia follows him every where he goes. John shares a split personality of an American FBI agent (Ed Harris) who needs John's assistance in decoding a secretive, Soviet attack. Along side the split personality of the agent is a party-driven roommate from college (Paul Bettany), and the roommate's young niece who exhibits John's innocence. Shooting out of Princeton, John receives a career with the Pentagon and is a teacher for those aspiring to be like him - especially one student. John meets and marries one of his pupils, Alicia (Jennifer Connely), who is his only source of strength and comfort as his condition hits hard, and nearly ruins him.

Russel Crowe gives a stunning performance as a mentally disturbed man who learns to live with his looming condition. Crowe proves how to take a true story of a man's life gently and carry it out with care and admiration. 

Knowing the same ideals of respect and care for a story is Ron Howard excellent direction. Howard brings forth a heart-warming, but at points, a heart-wrenching story. Mixing emotion and suspense, Howard's work of art is sensitive and wonderful.

This movie has moments where  it feels unengaging and I thought the film missed the mark in terms of getting inside the mind of John Nash, since it focused more on the results that his mind produced, but it eventually emerged as a feel-good, goosebumps causing crowd-pleaser. The last 30 minutes were especially engaging and brilliant because of the direction and acting. This film is a biopic based on the book of the same name. It's about a mathematician named John Nash (Russel Crowe) who becomes a paranoid schizophrenic. The first hour and a half covers Nash's college days and early career while intertwining scenes that completely take place in his head. After that Nash is treated at a hospital for his mind disorders and he would never be exactly the same again. Like I said, the movie really comes alive in the last half hour and those final scenes sealed the deal for this movie's Best Picture win. One other criticism I had for this movie is that it's a tad too long. They could have easily edited a few scenes out, but that was a minor problem. Overall this is an enjoyable and well made movie that has moments of greatness.

For me, this is one of Russell Crowe's finest performances, but the structure of the film is what makes it so good. 

As mere spectators, we find ourselves halfway through the film and still clinging to a thought that maybe, just maybe, Nash isn't mad at all; that he's going to turn out to be right after all. In other words, we find ourselves in his position, unable to tell what's really true and what's not. It's only when he finally accepts his illness that we too give up all hope that he could be justifiably paranoid, and from that point onwards it's a question of how to handle the situation. 

It's an impressive and effective technique, one that's followed up by something of a tear-jerking crescendo of an ending that's as happy as it possibly can be.

Ron Howard's conventional, middle-of-the-road biopic about Nobel Prize-winning mathematician John Nash, Jr. (Russell Crowe) who suffered from schizophrenia. Adapted from the Sylvia Nasar book, Akiva Goldsman's script oversimplifies mental illness. The rough edges of Nash's messy domestic life have been subdued, omitting that Nash fathered a child out of wedlock so as not to offend anyone. Nash's marriage to his MIT student, Alicia Larde (Jennifer Connelly), is fraudulently presented to suggest that mental illness can be overcome by the love of a good woman. There are scenes with flashy effects that show Nash's hallucinations, but a subplot involving a military officer (Ed Harris) who wants Nash to decode Soviet messages is a contrivance to goose the movie with suspense. "A Beautiful Mind" feels like a bland, inspirational disease of the week TV movie with a glossy look and Howard lays on the sentimentality when Nash gives an acceptance speech for the Nobel Prize. Crowe gives a showy, highly mannered performance similar to Dustin Hoffman in "Rain Man". The mind is really a fascinating organ. It's fair to say that my mind can't wrap itself around 'the mind' entirely.  How does it really work? Forget synapses and neurotransmitters and blah blah blah ...zzzzzzzz Oh no, I've bored myself.     :)     I thought I said it was fascinating??      Well it is!     But my pee-brain has trouble staying focused if you get too technical.    (lol)    This movie, thankfully, kept me entertained throughout.

  The film begins in the 1940's in Princeton, yes, New Jersey... ah another reason I like it.     :)   We meet John Nash (Crowe) a shall we say, um,... 'socially challenged' grad student at Princeton University.  He's struggling to find a unique mathematical theory, something with which he would stand alone and be recognized.  Now the "odd-duck mathmetician" label seems nothing out of the ordinary. Pretty standard stereotype which I am guilty myself of holding. (might have something to do with my disdain for mathematics...    :)   But John Nash is special indeed and the film carries us through 40 years or so of his life. 

Far from a movie about mathematics, thank God.    :)    This movie is about true love and commitment, how a mind works, it's relativity to the heart, with a little espionage and intrigue to boot.  Ron Howard directed this film and deserves all the accolades for creating a clever visual trip into one man's troubled mind.  So many subtle shots that almost go unnoticed. (The birds didn't fly away while the little girl was running near them...  and so on and so on)

Instead of Hollywood's usual interpretation of what true love is, this film was a refreshing break. It isn't all flowers and poems. When the film was released, Professor John Forbes Nash still worked at Princeton after he won his Nobel prize and still walked to work everyday. B is for A Beautiful Mind. 
John Nash (Russell Crowe) enters Princeton in 1947, sharing the prestigious Carnegie Award with Martin Hansen (Josh Lucas). After months of skipping class, preferring to hang out in the library with his roommate Charles (Paul Bettany), Nash finally earns his salt by developing the Nash Equilibrium of governing dynamics. He finishes his doctorate and begins teaching the eager young minds at MIT, including the beautiful Alicia (Jennifer Connelly), whom he begins dating and eventually marries. But not all is quiet on the western front, as Nash is recruited to secret government work by William Parcher (Ed Harris), spending more and more of his time seeking codes in magazines and newspapers and less of it on his official job at MIT. As Nash slips more and more into delusion, the world around him becomes more and more hostile, until eventually he has to be forcibly admitted to a psychiatric hospital. There he is told that Charles, Parcher, and his government mission are all figments of his imagination, part of his schizophrenia. He undergoes months of primitive electroconvulsive therapy and is started on medications, with a few relapses and never true control of all his symptoms. However, after many years of struggling with his illness, he is able to return to Princeton, even working again as a professor. And of course his earliest stroke of genius eventually earns him a Nobel Prize, leading to an enthralling biography and a Hollywoodized biopic - this film.
I remember seeing this movie when it first came out, and sadly, time and experience have not been kind to it. There are still moments that shine brilliantly: building a tie design, inspiration from a blonde, drawing umbrellas in the stars...in fact most of the Alicia-John romance. But the film is long and much of it is plodding, the story is sugar-coated beyond recognition and the medicine is dramatized to the point of blatant inaccuracy. Still, the cast is quite good and the music remains a definite highlight.
Overall, an over-simplified and none-too-accurate biopic of brilliant economist John Nash that is already starting to fade after only 9 years...but then again, who would have paid to see the true biography?

The mind is a very fragile piece of the human psyche, and sometimes it can turn against you, even if your mind is one of the most brilliant in the world. That is the basis of Ron Howard's A Beautiful Mind, balancing engrossing romanticism and surreal aspects to create a very interesting depiction of John Nash. What i must say about this movie first off is that it is pure Oscar bait and a conventional Hollywood drama. The musical score is familiar and the emotional scenes with the tug-at-your heart-strings lines are very cliche and expected. But what sets this apart is the astonishing performances from the cast. Russell Crows is a wonder as John Nash. Watching his world slowly fall apart, come back together and repeat sends waves of reality and heart over the viewer. Jennifer Connely is also exceptional as Nash's wife who just won't give up on him as a human being. When Nash's reality starts to fade, so does the movie's credibility. Sometimes, this film tries to hard to bring you into the illusions and madness that Nash is experiencing. There are also instances where you wish the music in the background would just stop playing as it over-dramatizes everything that is happening on the screen. Still, the direction is very sweeping and uplifting, the performances are stunning, and many of the scenes in this movie are very memorable. A Beautiful Mind stays too close to Hollywood conventions for me to call it a great film, but the weaving of a love story with a depiction of mental illness is a sign of some serious talent.

The performances basically make the movie what it is. I personally think this is Crowe's best performance. He inhabits Nash with a very scatter-brained approach, but he doesn't come off as some vegetable you would find in a mental hospital. You know that he has genuine emotions and feelings, but does not know how to express them. This makes it very easy to root or Nash and the hope that he will be at ease with his mind. Jennifer Connelly is also dazzling as his wife who just won't give up on what he is doing. Her faith in Nash along with her will power to keep her sanity as a wife and mother is courageous and Connelly takes the cliche script to new heights. We also have Ed Harris as the man in black who needs Nash to help break a code that the Russians are using to plan an attack on America. We also have some great work from Josh Lucas, Adam Goldberg, Christopher Plummer and Paul Bettany. The cast is great, and scenes that could have easily fell flat due to the overly dramatic script are buoyed by all of the performances. It is all the people that interact with Nash that try to help him reach back to find reality.

The direction by Ron Howard is nothing really too memorable, but its good. As i said, he just follows the usual great direction that is going to win Oscars. With Apollo 13, Howard did some wonderful work with the space sequences especially when the astronauts were weightless, and that story i found a tad bit more involving than this one. However, Howard does a great job with the surreal sequences actually bending the viewers mind and asking what is real and what is not. Sometimes you hope for reality and sometimes you hope for illusions, but he keeps you guessing which is the key. My wish is that Howard actually took some more risks with the camera shots an actors. Everything just seems formulaic with this one. Like i could guess how the next scene would be set up. Ron Howard does some interesting things here, but in the end, he's still sticking to the formula that always gets big attention.

The writing here is the movies problem. While around a halfway point a twist comes in that is very good, after that t just seems so predictable as to hat's going to happen. There is also some foreshadowing early in the movie that is way too obvious and i found myself knowing that certain scenes were going to be of importance later on. And sure enough they were. Im not going to spoil any of the big plot points, but the beginning of the movie was very good and I was highly interested in what Nash was doing, then after the halfway point you can see everything coming. Granted, its a long movie at 2 hours 15 minutes, but it breezed by to me. I will say that the script always has some interesting lines here and there, but, once again, a script that is predictable and cliche always wins.

I couldn't help but wish that A Beautiful Mind got me a little more than it did. The acting talent here is off the character and there is some ample direction to go with it, but the cliche script and predictability bring this film down a bit. I still like this movie very much because the story itself and the characters are so well done, but i want to see risks and reward. Crowe and the cast are game, and they make the movie more emotional than it should have been which i really enjoyed. A Beautiful Mind has all the Hollywood conventions you know, but beautiful performances merge seamlessly to make a beautiful love story

Ron Howard's heartfelt biography of Nobel Prize winner John Nash is driven by Russell Crowe's, Jennifer Connelly's, and Ed Harris' memorable performances and is an interesting look into mental illness, yet it does not succeed as a biographical film. John Nash (Russell Crowe), a mathematical prodigy at Princeton, has found himself on an avid pursuit to discover a truly original mathmatical idea. In the process of his thinking, Nash finds that he cannot get along with other students at the school or his flamboyant roommate (Paul Bettany). After college, Nash becomes a teacher at MIT, begins to help the Pentagon solve hidden codes, then he meets a girl (Jennifer Connelly) who he eventually marries. As time progresses though, Nash receives a steady rise in paranoia and becomes psychologically controlled by a Pentagon operative (Ed Harris) who wants to use him as a decoder against the Russians. Nash attempts to rebel, but he finds that he is dealing with something that he cannot comprehend on his own.

Ron Howard makes the film very likable and touching, as well as showing many raw emotions. There's a mound of cliches that drive the focus away from John Nash and towards his mental illness. The cliches break the seriousness and believability into this biographical film becoming more of a feel-good-movie. The script is blunted by the cliches and this causes a lack of character depth, which does succeed in being likable but not in being true to life. Ron Howard takes this blunted script and makes a sappy film with great acting.

Russel Crowe is just amazing. Crowe is incredibly likable when he acts as timid and paranoid John Nash, and Howard's direction turns him into a soaring, vibrant character. Jennifer Connelly gives a good performance which is highlighted by a few scenes, Ed Harris and Paul Bettany are beyond perfect for their roles because of their audacity, and Adam Goldberg makes another very good Woody Allen impression. 

Despite its biographical errors, A Beautiful Mind is brought to life by Russell Crowe's stellar performance, memorable characters, and a well told sympathetic story. 79/100

The film itself is as intelligent as the man behind "A Beautiful Mind:" John Forbes Nash Jr.
"This biographical piece of John Forbes Nash Jr. fails to show any weaknesses, only the weaknesses that this brilliant, but asocial man had to overcome in becoming the Nobel Prize Winner for Mathematics in 1994."
 
 The life that was, John Forbes Nash Jr, is such a deep and overly powerful story because of the mental hardships he had to overcome in being a top contributor to the world of mathematics. Russell Crowe's Oscar-Nominated performance (honestly, he should have won it over Denzel Washington in Training Day) makes the unstable madman that was Nash grow into a more stable, yet obsessively smart mathematician.  Crowe then grows some more into this man to the point where the viewer looks at Nash as a normal, but still genuinely genius at the time where he receives his Nobel Prize. Crowe's performance along with Ron Howard's effective cast and direction (especially the direction that featured the horrors of Nash's schizophrenia, those were quite intense) make this film a triumph-of-a biography. This film's well-deserved thoughtfulness was rewarded with the Best Picture at the 2001 Oscars.  The man that was John Forbes Nash Jr. will now be remembered more deeply by the public because of the success of this movie.     

Watching the film, you cannot help yourself in becoming so fascinated and intrigued by how John Forbes Nash, a Paranoid Schizophrenic, is able to overcome this profoundly dangerous mental illness, and only go on and do something that will get you a hell-of-a-lot of respect: Winning a Nobel Prize for Mathematics. Not only is the story of this man so intriguing, but every single piece of the actual film is nothing that I couldn't take my eyes or ears away from. The supporting cast behind the life of John Nash is superbly acted with the right amount of raw emotionally-generated resonance. Not to also mention that the delusional characters that only Nash could see were rightfully evil in trying to make them more believable to him despite Nash's failed attempts in trying to make them go away.  They played the horrors that drove the genius to the brinks of the mental institution, where he was given necessary treatment. All in all, never again will I go through my days in math without thinking of the math genius that was, John Forbes Nash Jr.

Plus, cinema and storytelling in general, at least for me, is not bound by reality. A fictional story is allowed poetic license by its very nature AS a piece of fiction. For those who want the historically faithful as possible account of Nash's life? The book's always going to be there. In the mean time, this is one of the rare cases where I'm praising Ron Howard's direction. Typically, Howard produces workman-like films with little visual flair. This one FINALLY features dynamic, wonderfully-assured direction that effortlessly pulls spectators through this kaleidescope of a story. Acting is brilliant all-around. Cinematography is excellent. And the score by James Horner is almost transcendental in its beauty. An amazing film that absolutely deserved the Best Picture Oscar.

As a person living with mental illness, I would recommend the movie "A Beautiful Mind". The film was about a man's ascension in the mathematical community, descent into his own world of paranoid schizophrenia, and ultimate heroic accomplishments while accepting his symptoms and being able to disengage himself from his delusions and hallucinations. John Nash, the movies' main character, proves he is sophisticated as well as a brave man in his quest to overcome his symptoms of mental illness while struggling to make a name for himself among collegiate peers that were considered the elite of this country's great minds. This movie also demonstrated a historical perspective in respect to therapeutic measures of the past treatment of schizophrenia. The family structure demonstrated in the movie provided an accurate and sophisticated viewpoint of how families of the time period possessed ways and means for recovery. The role of the professional in regards to the psychiatrist provided insight into symptoms associated with schizophrenia in relation to educating both patient and their families. In conclusion, John Nash proved through his Beautiful Mind, that a person living with schizophrenia does not have to settle with the struggles of daily hallucinations and proved that he could achieve amongst the highest nobility of men.

I watched this movie once before, with Spacky perhaps, back when I was 16 or so.  It was one of those movies that I had hailed as a masterpiece, and I had always referred to it fondly in my mind.  I wanted to see if I shared that same viewpoint upon watching it again.  Sad news is... this time around, I found this movie to drag on at times.  Many scenes were too gray and dull for me (reminded me too much of the very non-summer weather here) and I kept going to scenes which I knew were coming in my head and wanting them to arrive sooner: the part where John Nash is seen shouting to himself in the middle of the crowded college avenue, the scene where he enters the shack in the woods and finds a bunch of imaginary soldiers and their radio transistors set up. 
     
Maybe I didn't notice this before, but I actually kind of found John Nash to be a rather unlikeable guy.  From the get-go, with all of his refusal to make eye contact and his shuffling demeanor, it seemed that he had some other social/mental condition in addition to the schizophrenia.  That's the kind of person he was, I guess, and it's odd how I never remembered that about the movie.  It's a wonder that his wife in this movie (thoroughly Hollywood) put up with him so beautifully.  I could relate to her more because of how she had to go through that - and her experience made a point of showing just how messed up a sane person's life can be when they love somebody who is literally crazy.
     
This being a movie largely made up for the sake of the film (and not real life), some of the "magic" that would have gone with a true story was lost.  Upon wondering why Nash hallucinated three specific people, I had to stop to remind myself that these characters came from the mind of the director, not Nash.  The real Nash hallucinated vague angels and aliens and voices from the sky that talked to him - not actual people who looked as real as anybody else.  Which is really too bad.  I would have asked why he imagined a roommate, a little girl, and a bald man connected with the CIA, and wondered why John couldn't just privately talk with these imaginary figures as opposed to completely shutting them out of his head in the end.  It would've been like having an entire conversation with different sides of yourself!  How neat!
     
Throughout the movie, I tried to look for physical signs that the characters in Nash's head were not real, knowing that they were made up.  The most obvious one was where his "prodigal roommate"s niece goes running around on one of the lawns of the college, where birds are standing - the birds do not move when she runs near them, as she isn't really there to chase them off.  And really, the other characters handily stepped off screen when any real characters showed up, effectively cutting off any chance that there would be an awkward scenario where he'd illicit strange stares from his actual friends.
     
It was lovely that Nash had the friends he needed to keep him grounded in the world that he lived in.  The scenes featuring the depths of his madness were scary - the number planted beneath his skin that changed (what kind of sci-fi future is that?!), the letters piled up in the mail box (reminiscent of Grandad's madness), the black cars that circled (I just saw a sleek, darkened window mafia looking car driving slowly through my neighborhood with a license plate that read "X-ray 1" and it creeped me out so bad).  Any sane person would react the same way to the things that he experienced.  But we all, as an audience, wind up rooting for Nash simply because he is the hero of this story.  Bumbling and unaware that he is of his social appearance, his gift to the world was and is a step toward healing humankind of its competitive, backstabbing ways.
     
I am glad I have come full circle with this movie, dissipating the idealistic illusions I had about it being one of the best films I have ever seen.  It has fallen toward the medium circle for me, with its long drawn out dark scenes and brooding interludes.  I guess maybe I am a quicker paced person than I thought I was.

Russell Crowe is fantastically brilliant in Ron Howard's masterpiece, A Beautiful Mind. This is a film that I did not expect to like as much as I did, but I found myself loving every minute of it and unable to tear myself away from the screen lest I miss a moment of its brilliance.

A Beautiful Mind was a true story, something I didn't realize going into it. I think that until the first half of the movie was over, I was a little cautious of some of this movie. For instance, this seemed to be a film about a mathematical genius who works for the government, but is soon hunted down by some sort of conspiracy. I'm sure I've seen this story already somewhere else before... But when the story shows itself for what it truly is, well, that's when it really got interesting.

There are themes explored here that I haven't seen before. And a love story present here that I haven't seen before either. And I think that's probably my favorite part of A Beautiful Mind. I think I have seen one too many biographical films in which the husband has a problem of some kind, whether it's a mental problem or drug problem or what have you, and the wife gets fed up with his shenanigans and leaves his ass behind. That doesn't happen here. I'd hate to give that away, but the fact that she doesn't leave him but instead remains a devoted and loving wife is so uplifting and fresh, that I found that to be my favorite part of the picture. And it shows the wife to be a much stronger character than the audience is use to the wife being. I'm sure some feminists would disagree and say it would take a stronger woman to leave her "no-good" husband, but the fact that this woman breaks that archetype makes so much more interesting and profound than any movie wife I think I have ever seen.

Something else I loved about this movie was its way of toying with the audience's perception of reality to illustrate the main character's own loss of sense of reality. It's a very scary feeling that the John Nash goes through, and taking the audience on this journey becomes one of the best parts of the picture's strengths.

And the direction is absolutely spectacular. There are so many ways this story could have gone wrong. I am thinking of the way the film Radio was treated. This could have just been another Radio (well, first Radio, I guess, since this film was made first), but it wasn't. This was a movie that focused on the character, not the disorder. It does balance both for the most part, but at no point in the film is the audience invited to feel pity on this character for being handicapped. It's just a smart, smart film.

A Beautiful Mind was a wonderful experience. It's not a film I could watch again and again, but it doesn't have to be. Being just a film that can be watched once and loved for the rest of my life based on that one experience is enough to keep me more than satisfied. But it's a brilliantly told story, and that's what makes it so good. This is a film that's all about abandoning laziness.

This film has schizophrenia. 

It really makes you immersed into the paranoia and delusional mindset of John Nash Jr., that guy who said economics was a game and earned a Nobel prize for that. You think that for minutes on end that characters like Charles and Parcher actually exist - however, if defined correctly, Charles was made from John's desire for a friend and Parcher was made to embody the building Cold War-era paranoia of his teaching days. Oh, that girl who always calls him Uncle John? Maybe his longing for a child - which is why she becomes prevalent in the later part of the film - or the fact that he needs to flesh out Charlie.

Great acting, great writing, great directing, and a great, laid-back production scale. This deserves Best Picture - and don't come to me saying that "Amelie" deserved it. It may be French, more creative, and funnier, but Ron Howard put it all together here.

But did we need an overdose of Parcher? Guy was a jerk from the beginning - and did we need his imaginary friends puffing up at him when he's trying to ignore them in his later life? Not really - Ron should've made Charles, his niece, and Parcher turn to John and smile, knowing that they helped him go towards his advances in game theory, not act like the ghosts they are. But that's copping out for the Hollwood ending.

So, yeah. This is a pretty perfect film.

Based on the true story of genius mathematician John Nash, "A Beautiful Mind" is a compelling drama film by Ron Howard starring Russell Crowe, Ed Harris, and  Jennifer Connelly. The film basically centers on Nash, and it's through his discoveries in tracking a and breaking codes that we see just how convoluted the mystery in "A Beautiful Mind" really is. Because the story is fairly simple, the film relies on good directing techniques and sharp performances to carry it. Crowe does a hell of a job. And it is a crime he did not win the Oscar--even though it had it been a year after "Gladiator."The depth he adds to Nash just by sitting and staring into space, or walking with a gimp-like crawl, or lets not forget that western accent he put on so well. Crowe's performance is what made and, often, saved the movie. There are a few scenes where you can' quite pin-point what it is that's going on, and when you learn of the real tragedy, all of what you just saw feels like recycled drama almost--but, it's not. And again that's because the film survives so well due to Crowe you can actually feel your in is mind on a couple of scenes. You feel his frustration, especially in scenes with Connelly, who he marries in the film. The lack of enthusiasm to be a parent Crowe displays, a scene shows him sitting morosely with the baby crying and screaming in his arms. It's quite sad, and it's the moments like that of this film that make it unique, and also the fact that it's based on a true story. I think "A Beautiful Mind" is both Howard and Crowe's best, and deserves all the acclaim it received. It's a touching and overall enjoyable film, with the same sort of heart past Academy Award winners had such as "Rain Man" or "American Beauty."-- one of the better films of the first half of the 2000s.

Russell Crowe stars in the most magnificent movie of the modern era.  Weve seen Crowe act in other types of movies like Gladiator, Robin Hood, and Cinderella Man, but this time, Crowe doesnt blow us away with his great action sequences, he stuns us with his brilliant acting. 

In the Ron Howard directed movie A Beautiful Mind, set in the late 1940s, Crowe acts the part of John Nash. From the very beginning, we see this socially awkward yet mathematical genius develop at Princeton University. He is said to have had two helpings of brain but only a half helping of heart, Nash will struggle with this for the remainder of the film. Nash can discover logical mathematical meaning for various situations, from a formula of people playing touch football to an algorithm for the movement of pigeons.  But this is where the struggle starts; he is so logical that he cant function well with people, especially women. He tends to be extremely forward and doesnt beat around the bush. He puts things in his own terms; he gets to the desired result as soon as possible. Which we all know with the more delicate sex, takes time, and for Nash, a slap in the face.

Eventually, Nash moves on from graduate school and is able to find the perfect wife, Alicia, excellently acted by Jennifer Connelly. She is almost as logical as Nash, and understands how his mind works. He starts to progress in his career and build a family. But a secret service has been watching Nash and discovers his incredible ability to crack codes. He, then, is ordered to help decipher Russian messages.  The secret agent named Parcher, played by Ed Harris, is able to manipulate Nash to accomplish his work, no matter the cost. But because this work is classified, Nash is forced to secrecy from his wife. 

Then all of our hearts drop, just as Nashs, when we find out that he has been diagnosed with schizophrenia. This is a news flash to everyone in the audience also, as this is happening, we are as much in denial as Nash is. And this is the beauty of Howards directing; we are going through the story as Nash is going through it, we dont know whats real, we dont know whats fake.  We are trying to solve this problem as Nash is trying to solve it.

The Schizophrenia gets so bad that Nash almost hurts his family. We all know he means the best, but he cant figure out what is actually there, and whats in his mind. This is especially difficult for Nash because there has never been a problem that he couldnt solve. Since Princeton, he was editing some of the most world renowned and complicated mathematical formulas. But when we discover that the problem IS his mind, we realize that Nashs beautiful mind cant solve this one.

I dont know if its Crowes acting or Howards directing, but this is a spectacular film. Howard takes us through this breathtaking true story of genius, heart, depression and achievement, and Crowe makes it personal. With his acting, we are pulled into the movie, putting us in his place. We, as the audience, start to wonder what has been real this whole time and what has never existed in the first place.  We dont know whom to believe. We dont know who isnt there. As Nash struggles with it, we struggle too. This is the brilliance of Crowes work; with his glorious acting he plays Nash perfectly. From his socially awkward college days, to his most confused, Crowe does it all. 

If you know your history well, you already know the ending, if you were like me and didnt know what the movie was about before you put it in, Im not going to spoil it for you. Its a fantastic movie everyone should watch. Your mind is constantly working through this movie, and thats what makes it so beautiful. The second its over you want to watch it again. As you finish the movie, you dont know if the real genius was Nash, or if it was Crowe.

A Beautiful Mind is definitely the type of movie that wins over the academy every year. They've always had a thing for heart string dramas, and while they don't always pick the best film per say, I truly believe this one deserved the win back in 2001. Many films grow a hatred after thet win awards, due to the fact that people now find them overrated, when they just didn't really think it was good enough to win. The term overrated is overused nowadays, but that's just my opinion. Happily, A Beautiful Mind is one of the films that I don't hear many complaints about as time as gone by. Sure, there are a few manipulative scenes and certain people who have direct relations to this film may not love it as much as some people, but I for one feel as though this film still stands as a masterpiece, and here's why. 

The watching this film for the first time, it feels like three completely different films throughout its three act structure. The first act feels more like it's going to be a movie in the same vein as Good Will Hunting, only to become a much more thrilling film, dealing with a nuclear bomb investigation throughout its second, eventually throwing the audience through a loop, making them wonder if anything they had just seen really happened at all. Once you've seen A Beautiful Mind, the surprises won't ever be there again, but the emotion is still very much present and worth watching over and over again. Russell Crowe is a revelation throughout this movie, plain and simple.

Plain and simple, this film wouldn't have worked as well without a performance as devoted as Russell Crowe's. His mannerisms and the way he's able to fall in love with Alicia (Jennifer Connelly), is truly what transcends the film, making it as emotional as it is when the final act begins. His performances sucks you in from the very beginning and never lets you go, having you feel completely invested in this real-life character that had gone and still continues to go through this until the day the film was released. Across the board, this film is so well-acted, that it would've even been effective with a terrible screenplay, but that's just not the case at all. 

When it comes to screenwriting, it's very hard to make even the most realistic dialogue naturally flow as if you're watching something unfold in reality, but this is one of the few films that will always remain in my memory as a movie with a perfect screenplay. From the moments that need you to feel for each character in order to hold your interest, to the subtle moments that talk about love in great detail, to the seemingly overdone scientific subplots, once all is revealed in this film, everything falls into place perfectly, leaving nothing else to be desired, at least for myself. 

From performances, to superb direction by Ron Howard, to a script that will have those invested in tears, to a score that pulled me right into every moment, A Beautiful Mind won all of those awards for a reason. Looking back on this movie, nothing stands out as dated, even though it's only about 16 years old. If you've yet to view this film, I can't recommend it enough, especially to those who are fans of the dramatic side of filmmaking. I whole-heartedly love this movie for all of these reasons and then some. It's stylistic editing choices and use of on-set effects help this film feel even more authentic than it's script would've already allowed it to, so I have nothing to complain about in retrospect. This is a beautiful movie.

A big part of this film is the repeated encounters that Nash has with some imaginary characters who influence his decisions. The film attempts to put the viewer into his headspace, experiencing the things which he is experiencing and not knowing what is real and what is not. It really does play games with your mind, but that is what makes this film work so well in the end.

2001 film based on the life of John Forbes Nash, Jr., a Nobel Laureate in Economics. The film was directed by Ron Howard and written by Akiva Goldsman. It was inspired by a bestselling, Pulitzer Prize-nominated 1998 book of the same name by Sylvia Nasar. The film stars Russell Crowe, along with Jennifer Connelly, Ed Harris, Christopher Plummer and Paul Bettany.
The story begins in the early years of a young schizophrenic prodigy named John Nash. Early in the movie, Nash begins developing paranoid schizophrenia and endures delusional episodes while painfully watching the loss and burden his condition brings on his wife and friends.
The film opened in US cinemas on December 21, 2001. It was well-received by critics, grossed over $170 million worldwide, and went on to win four Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Supporting Actress. It was also nominated for Best Leading Actor, Best Editing, Best Makeup, and Best Score. The film has been criticized for its inaccurate portrayal of some aspects of Nash's life. The film fictionally portrayed his hallucinations as visual and auditory, when in fact they were exclusively auditory. Also, Nasar concluded that Nash's refusal to take drugs "may have been fortunate," since their side effects "would have made his gentle re-entry into the world of mathematics a near impossibility"; in the screenplay, however, just before he receives the Nobel Prize, Nash speaks of taking "newer medications."

Anyone who has not seen this film really ought to, as it is probably the best representation of schizophrenia ever committed to the silver screen. I will go into the story a little bit, if you will just indulge me a little.

It is the 1940's and eccentric loner John Forbes Nash, Jr. has just been accepted into Princeton University, to join the legion of mathematicians that will direct the course of the war. He doesn't fit in, and isn't taken seriously by his classmates. However, he finds solace in his dear friend Charles, who likes to do things his own way, and always lends a listening ear to John's thoughtful ranting. 

John struggles to find his "truly original idea" so he can distinguish himself and earn respect, and he is torn between recognition and accomplishment. He does become successful, and we go forward a few years. He has been hired by the government to crack some very elaborate ad tough codes, which have something to do with a top secret nuclear weapon. On the side, he is back at Princeton teaching the eager young minds of tomorrow and it is here he meets the beautiful, confident and ambitious Alicia, who takes a liking to him. 

The two fall in love and their relationship flourishes, however John's work is getting darker and more dangerous and pretty soon he's convinced there are people after him. He becomes paranoid, fearful and shaken... but is it actually happening to him? This is where the film takes a major turn, revealing a deep secret that changes the life of John Nash forever. 

There are so many great elements to this movie. First off, it is carried all the way by the brave and mesmerizing performance of Russell Crowe. You really believe he is going through this journey, and we are taken into his world of theories and ideas, in a beautiful and haunting way by the ever versatile director of the film, Ron Howard.

When this film came out, Russell Crowe had just become an overnight star after the 2000 success of Gladiator. The 2002 Oscars were just around the corner and at the time, Rusty had reaped almost every award that he had been nominated for and the final statuette at the Academy Awards was surely looking like it would go to him. Of course, he didn't win it, however his performance has to be one of the best of the decade. 

This was when I really started to become a Russell Crowe fan; I must have seen Gladiator about 10 times, and was digging deep into Crowe's resume to discover his lesser known and earlier works from Australia. Some roles were pretty standard, and then there were other groundbreaking performances in such films as 'Romper Stomper', 'The Insider' and 'LA Confidential'. 

Later on that year, when A Beautiful Mind came to DVD I purchased it straight away and watched it several times; it still captivated me. I then began to explore the special features and was impressed even more when I saw what Ron Howard went through to bring his vision to the screen. I won't go into detail but it reminded me of what a truly gifted filmmaker he is and when you watch the features and then the film and put it all together, you will understand and agree with me that A Beautiful Mind isn't just a movie, it is a piece of art. 

It has inspired me to believe that the mind is an incredibly powerful thing, that can help us have, do and be anything, but in the end there is only one thing more powerful than the mind... and that is the courage of the heart. 

Truly a film to be cherished.

A Beautiful Mind is a beautifully constructed film that is both emotionally fullfilling and strongly cerebral.  It's another Award Winning film from Ron Howard who has transformed himself into one of the best directors in the game, anything he is associated with ends up being a steller piece of work, A Beautiful Mind is no exception. "A Beautiful Mind", which was inspired by the biography of the same name by Sylvia Nasar, has nothing to do with the real John Nash, Jr. who won the Nobel Prize in 1994.  What we have here is an impostor, a fictional character with the same name as the real John Nash yet director Ron Howard, screenwriter Akiva Goldsman and company have taken it upon themselves to tell his story much like the actual events complete with title cards at the end of the film stating where Mr. Nash and his wife currently resides and what they are presently doing.

The real John Nash is a complex, difficult and at times, a selfish and insensitive individual.  What the filmmakers have concocted here is a work of fantasy (forget fiction).  It neither belongs to the real John Nash nor to the psychiatric profession as it inaccurately depicts the schizophrenic condition.  Expunged, among other things, are his arrogant, rude and sarcastic behavior; his mistress Eleanor and his illegitimate son; his homosexual relationships; his arrest for indecent exposure; his divorce from his wife Alicia and his involuntary commitments to numerous psychiatric hospitals.  His delusions about messages from alien creatures are replaced by espionage and spying only to give the film dramatic weight and tension.  The film also takes dramatic license as to the timing of his mental illness.

With a subject matter that tackles the brilliance and genius of a real life mathematician and his bout with schizophrenia, it is ironic how Ron Howard would insult the intelligence of his audience by dumbing down certain events about the real John Nash.  Is he afraid that audiences will be unable to handle the truth and honesty about John Nash's life and still be sympathetic to him and his condition?  From the get-go, Howard gives us a character that is so likeable unlike the real Nash just so that the audience will automatically care for him despite his mental illness.

However, even with all these faults, Mr. Howard certainly knows how to push the right buttons as most people unfamiliar with schizophrenia and John Nash will ignore these inaccuracies and omissions of fact and still embrace the film.  This is the type of film that mainstream audiences love with hardly a single curse word and a happy ending.  Expect the Academy to do the same come Oscar time.

What the film has going for it is the fine performances of its two leads Russell Crowe and Jennifer Connelly.  However, there were times where Mr. Crowe would speak at a very low unmannered voice that one could barely hear what he is saying.

It is very ironic that another film that I would also have problems with its historical inaccuracies and omissions of fact would also star Mr. Crowe himself - Michael Mann's "The Insider".

"A Beautiful Mind" avoids the complexity, turmoil and harsh realities of its subject matter.  Contrary to what the filmmakers would like you to believe, the screenplay DOES NOT capture the essence of the story.  "A Beautiful Mind" could have been a rich and powerful film of significant human interest.  But it isn't.  Strategically released on Christmas day, it does nothing more than lift one's spirits by using false notes.  It neither inspires nor educates.  It hardly even entertains.

A Beautiful Mind is a 2001 American film based on the life of John Forbes Nash, Jr., a Nobel Laureate in Economics. 
The film was directed by Ron Howard and stars Russell Crowe, along with Jennifer Connelly, Ed Harris, Christopher Plummer and Paul Bettany.

The story begins in the early years of a young schizophrenic prodigy named John Nash. Early in the film, Nash begins developing paranoid schizophrenia and endures delusional episodes while painfully watching the loss and burden his condition brings on his wife and friends.

I love life stories, I also heavily adore physiological movies, this technically is more of a biopic though.

I find the only downside to movies like this is, sometimes you think the climax has arrived and you think the film is done, then another ten minutes go by, something else extraordinary happens, and you're left waiting when his life is done? not because you want it to end, but a normal movie would have had more foreshadowing or build up.

Of coarse this is based on a real person, so I guess life really isn't like a movie, people have ups and downs.

Russell Crowe was a very tough nut to crack, at first, he seemed rather normal to me, and to be honest not that deep of a character, but the journey you and him go through in the span of his life shown on screen was truly amazing, My hat goes off to you sir.

Beautiful Mind grossed over $170 million worldwide, went on to win four Academy Awards, including Best Picture, 
Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, 
and Best Supporting Actress. 
It was also nominated for Best Leading Actor, Best Editing, Best Makeup, and Best Score. 

You can see very clearly why it won each of it's awards, it out stands alot of movies I've seen recently, & would definitely make my favorite movies category.

Overall 'A Beautiful Mind' shows us what mental illness can do the human being, this is shown through fantastic direction & stellar performances.

John Nash is a mathematician/student at Princeton, trying to discover an "original" mathematical equation that could break some new ground. He is able to do so, with the help of his roommate Charles. Beautiful mind... I can't breathe! I got a disease! Matchbox Twenty reference, anyone? A fall-flat, awkward opening joke? Either I'm going crazy too or my creative juices have taken a blow because of how effective the psychological impact is. Of course, the concept alone isn't going to deliver a hard enough psychological blow. Credit goes out to Ron Howard and Russell Crowe, but more on them later.

As good as the film is, it does suffer from a moderate lack of immediate development and a bit of a bumpy transition from the lengthy development segment. In spite of these small complaints, the film still features good dialogue, fine visual effects, very good make-up when aging comes into play, charming character chemistry and boasts a compelling story, strong characters, an exhilarating score, a solid twist, fantastic acting and very effective emotional and psychological impact. But what makes the impacts of this film so effective? Why, it's director Ron Howard, who once again brings his trademark grittiness to the film, which works to great effect when he brilliantly transports us into Crowe's character John Nash's situation and has us feeling his struggles - certainly not to an authentic extent - but still genuinely enough for us to feel his pain. Man, Ron could have us feel the pain of a mental patient and now he can't even make "The Da Vinci Code" complex. Maybe he's slipping into madness too. Did you really think I was going to review a great Ron Howard movie without complaining about one of his very few bad movies that he did years later?

But seriously though, as fantastic as Howard's direction is, he still can't pull off the film's emotional influence alone. Equal, if not more credit goes to leading man Russell Crowe for being the key ingredient to the film's immerseiveness. Crowe's smaller accomplishments in the performance - such as a likeable charisma and solid accent and mannerism changes - are impressive. His much grander accomplishments of emoting and giving off the genuine atmosphere of his character in order to complete Howard's emotional and psychological influence is downright beyond awe-inspiring. Really, I don't exactly know how to break down Crowe's - dare I say it - masterful performance. Perhaps the best word to fully convey the quality of Crowe's performance in this film is "transformation". He dives as deeply as ever into his role and masterfully transforms into his character, with the only evidence of his being, well, Russell Crowe being his distincitve appearance, voice and name for the book of acting legends in the credits.

Ultimately, "A Beautiful Mind", led by Ron Howard's incredible direction and Russell Crowe's show-stoppingly masterful performance - oh, I mean transformation, stands ever-so tall as a powerful and deeply moving retelling of the great John Nash's brilliance and struggles, as well as a fascinating study on the complexities of the human mind.

"A Beautiful Mind" is a great drama. It's based on the true story of John Nash, a brilliant mathemetician on the brink of international acclaim and success until he is visited by a man identifying himself as William Parcher, a federal agent who wants to recruit him to crack codes from Russian spies bent on destroying the United States. But it turns out that Nash is actually suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, and has been doing so for years. Even his best friend/ex-roommate, Charles, is nothing more than a creation of his imagination. Nash's gorgeous and devoted wife, Alicia, shows the true meaning of the marriage vow line "in sickness and in health". Frustrated and afraid, she still loves and sticks by her husband through his tumultuous mental issues and is the reason Nash really becomes who he becomes.

The acting is pretty superb. Jennifer Connelly is believable as Alicia, but I do have a hard time seeing how she'd find a guy like John Nash attractive enough to ask him out. He's smug, dismissive of others, and unkempt-- his fingernails are creepily long. John Nash is socially inept, odd, and amazingly arrogant about his own abilities but Russell Crowe actually manages to make that twitchiness a mildly endearing attribute. Endearing enough to make you root for Nash's recovery and success, and actually begin to hate the figments of his imagination (Charles, Parcher, even little Marcee) that threaten to bring him down.

Looking at the details of the DVD info, it had a few words for the film A Beautiful Mind because it wants to have us watch and enter to this delicate film.

One of the themes the film deals with is mental illness as the character is diagnosed, but we don't know that until we see the film. Sorry for the spoiler, you did not know that, but anywhere you look will have tell you what the film deals with.

A Beautiful Mind is the first I seen where schizophrenia was used correctly in terms of identification. The film is tagged based on a true story, so it will up the chances of someone believing although; one can question the adaptation over the film and John Nash. A number of shows and movies often get the characteristics of schizophrenia wrong like Me, Myself, & Irene. Schizophrenia means split mind, and it is widely believed that it means more than one personality. Wrong. It is classified as a mental disturbance that affect common life including social, thinking, emotions, and reality. Russell Crowe's character, John Nash, is a very smart man and very delicate except when it comes to the ladies in the bar. He attends the University of Princeton where he studies and concentrates a couple of theories. He is on the verge of success and accomplishing great things until he nearly loses it all. 

We open up with Nash in Princeton University as comes off normal with a few oddities. When reading the newspapers, words and numbers begin to fly out and connect with each other leading John to start puzzling and connecting the dots. John surrounds himself with newspapers and linking the article believing there is a secret code. He does not find it odd, but believe he is special or gifted. In reality, nothing is encoded and a regular person would have though he is crazy or on drugs. I would have personally played along; trying to see what is his major malfunction.
 
Throughout the first part of the movie, we see through John's view. He's a normal man with a gifted mind with math. His theories are very amazing and later become prolifically. You (audience and readers) can tell that he is not social especially when he uses one of the greatest pickup lines of all time, "exchange fluids?" The only thing I was fishy about was his friend and roommate Charles. Out of all the people, Charles is a person that John can talk to him without the awkwardness contrasting his personality in public. However, I did let my guard down as the story takes an awkward turn when John is chosen to help the Pentagon from Department of Defense. I still thought it was normal. There he meets William Parcher (William Harris) one of the agents of Department of Defense. His task is to find and decode the messages subliminally implanted in newspapers, whatever. The film switches to what is happening in real life and we are shocked. His wife investigates and sees another perspective to what has been really happening. The revelations are strong and too real. 

Though manipulated, we cannot wonder how this came about, but understand a fraction world of John Nash is in. No, I do not believe the film could be used as a prime example and saying, oh yeah, I know what schizophrenia is like! The screenwriter Akiva Goldsman and director Ron Howard try to capture and bring back the visual wonderful world of schizophrenia although it could be off depending who you ask. We feel for the character and grow with them as we believe that everything is true. Suddenly, his voices paranoia kicks when incidents involving Russians. We follow the character to survive in possible way as we rely on him because we are observing his point of view. We come to terms at the start of the revelations. We learn about schizophrenia through the doctors. I will leave it that with plot. 

A Beautiful Mind accomplishes a lot as we are given a great picture. The acting is really great allowing us to enter and feel the characters as we move. Mr. Crowe was excellent in the portrayal of Nash even though we don't really know how he is. We should be careful when using films portrayals of a real life person: movie's version vs. actual personality. Jennifer Connelly does a wonderful job as Alicia Nash, John's wife. Ed Harris was really intimidating the agent of Dept. of Defense. Everybody else was great thanks to the well written script and Ron Howard's direction. I believe we will never enter the world of schizophrenia and know it through the eyes of those, but a film like this will have us understand in a level.

A gripping, haunting and even ghostly biopic, I would rank A Beautiful Mind positively almost only because of its splendid cast. This was especially so with respect to Russell Crowe's role as John Forbes Nash. His performance was indeed very inspiring to see, and although certain very improbable liberties were taken with the representation of his character, they still accentuated his wretched and sympathetic plight. For instance, in reality, Nash didn't see see non-existent secret agents or a little girl: he just heard imaginary voices. However, paraphrasing the real Nash's own words, to depict only voices onscreen wouldn't have been dramatically convincing. Conjuring visions of imaginary people onscreen was, to the real Nash, an effective way of displaying the inner madness that was imprinted on his psyche throughout his career. He remains one of my most inspirational figures, and needless to say, Ron Howard made a beautiful biopic of his life in this. With one weakness, however - I felt that it was rather too long and drab, and at points, things even got a bit confusing (in an unnecessary way). Having said that, this was a very worthy biopic, and with that haunting James Horner score, it got even more inspiring and uplifting to watch.

It's disappointing how far off this film is from John Nash's life. However, as a film about the life of a mentally-ill genius, it is interesting in its portrayal of relationships, hubris, and change, but not necessarily in its depiction of mental-illness itself, which it likely portrays highly inaccurately. The film's strength is that it covers such a long period in this made-up Nash's life that it is able to show his relationship with himself and others change, which is insightful and interesting to watch. For example, A Beautiful Mind shows us that Nash is accepted only late in his life, when the people around him change and notice him through his work and not through his famed antics, which is an interesting observation. I'll also admit to completely being taken in by the film's nostalgia (and piling on much more nostalgia as well) and infectious somber atmosphere, but really these are some of the gaping flaws in this film, whose sentimentalism makes for a wondrous tale, but detracts from realism and prevents it from being a realistic tale about any mentally-ill genius, let alone a biographical tale about The John Nash.

Ron Howard directed this amazing movie that won 4 academy awards including best picture in the year of 2001.  I think that A Beautiful Mind is the best film that he has directed of the ones I have seen.  The film is a true story about a tortured genius named John Nash.  John Nash was a math genius, and a code breaker.  He was absolutely brilliant, and there was no code or pattern that he couldn't crack.  He was tortured because he is a schizophrenic.  He was paranoid until he learned it.  When he learned that he had it he eventually got better, but he never beat it entirely.  He still see's people that aren't there, but he ignores them and he moves on with his life.  The film goes through the story of his life from the years of 1947 - 1994.

At first John was kind of a stereotypical genius.  When he spoke he sounded as educated as it gets, and slightly arrogant at times.  He seemed like he thought he was above things at certain points, but that feeling I only had about once or twice.  He is the type of genius that doesn't have many other redeeming qualities other then his brains.  He is not very sociable, outgoing, or even relatable.  It is sad because not many people liked him, and he knew it.  He is fascinating to listen too, and I would love to meet a genius like him, because I am sure it would be a really interesting experience.  His genius was purely mathematical, and that he analyzed the world around him through math and algorithms.  He went to Princeton University in the year of 1947.  People picked on him for being weird, and he clearly was strange.  He never went to class because he thought, "Classes will dull your mind, destroy the potential for authentic creativity."  In his case he was right, and he did better by not going to class.  He would find algorithms for everything, and wrote them on the window of his dorm.  During the time he was at college he would do things like try to figure out how to spend the night with a girl who he met at a bar, but he wasn't any good at it.  He and his friends were always trying to figure out how to get with a girl, but he would always come up with some mathematical solution to it.  Five years later he is working at the Pentagon as an analyst.  He also worked at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and he had to teach their students to get the facilities that he wanted to work at.  That is how he met his future wife Alicia (Jennifer Connelly).  She actually asked him out, and the eventually got married.

His illness is something you are oblivious about until you are finally told about it.  Like all dramas it starts off happier then it really gets more serious when the conflict kicks in.  He had a roommate named Charles Herman (Paul Bettany) who was his best friend, that didn't exist.  That roommate he imagines has lots of personality, and eventually a niece named Marcee (Vivien Cardone), who never gets older.  That is how he earns that he doesn't actually see her.  They see each other regularly, but not so much that it isn't abnormal.  So that kind of makes it seem like they just ran into each other.  The big one was the man William Parcher who he imagined that he worked for.  William Parcher (Ed Harris) wanted him to help him decipher codes to a bomb that terrorists were going to detonate in America.  However Parcher was just a part of his imagination, and ash spent a ton of time deciphering codes in newspapers and magazines that didn't make sense.  The people he was imagining started to put him in danger, and he became really paranoid.

He was put in the hospital, where he got a lot of help.  When he got out he eventually started to see them again, and he put his baby in danger thinking that his old roommate who didn't exist was watching him.  Parcher came back and started to tell him about his work and he basically just relapsed.  He eventually realized that he was never going to beat it, so he decided just to ignore the three people who would always see, and he lived his life that way.  He and his wife are still alive today, and he still lives with his illness.  He will have to ask if a person is really there or not.  Once he learned of his illness that allowed him to get much better.
